113. First and Second Update [V]

In the end, Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin were selected.

They were selected based on their faces.

After returning to the capital to recuperate for a period of time, the two of them turned fair again. The border-killing atmosphere that made people shudder was added to their full scholarly temperament, making them like aged strong liquor, even more lingering in charm, and they fascinated countless women in the capital.

E'lundai: "Actually, they also fascinated many men. Many men asked them if they wanted to become brothers."

Yin Ti: "Wow, killing both men and women."

Yinreng: "Don't say it, Rongruo and Ziqing are going to take knives to hack you!"

Yin Ti put his hands on his hips: "I am a prince, who dares!"

E'lundai also put his hands on his hips: "I am a Heshuo Prince Consort, the Emperor's cousin, who dares!"

Yinreng: "..."

Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin: "..." They both had the urge to quit.

Others were selected for their martial arts, but they were selected because of their faces, and they were also repeatedly told by the Emperor to protect their faces, as their faces were the face of Great Qing.

Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin: "???"

What made them even more unacceptable was that because Westerners didn't like to keep beards and preferred handsome men with a youthful feel, in order to confuse Westerners with their faces, the handsome guard team they led all shaved their beards.

Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin: "..." They once suspected that the Emperor wanted to send them, a group of handsome and dashing noble sons, to foreign nobles as lovers.

But the imperial order could not be disobeyed, so they could only shave their beards, grow their hair, put on the tight-fitting prince honor guard uniforms specially customized by the tailors in the palace, use leather belts to squeeze out thin waists, and match them with a scimitar with a gem-encrusted gold scabbard.

The noblewomen in the capital were drooling uncontrollably as they watched the new military parade.

Kangxi was extremely satisfied: "This is the face of our Great Qing!"

Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin: "..." Your Majesty, could you please stop talking?

Isn't the face of the Great Qing supposed to be strong ships and powerful cannons? What does it have to do with our faces?

They turned their eyes toward the Crown Prince, the most reliable person they knew, seeking help.

Yinreng pinched his own delicate chin, looked up at Kangxi, and said, "I think our honor guard still needs more practice. Their appearance is sufficient, but their spirit and demeanor are still lacking."

Kangxi said, "The voyage to Europe will take nearly half a year. Use this time to train them well."

When Kangxi spoke of this duration, his fists tightened involuntarily.

With half a year for the round trip, plus the time spent on the diplomatic visit, Yinreng would likely not return for two or three years.

The moment Kangxi thought about the little Crown Prince, who was inseparable from him, leaving for such a long time, he felt the urge to stop Yinreng from going abroad.

But this diplomatic visit was far too important; the position the Great Qing would hold on the world stage in the future would basically be decided by these negotiations. Kangxi could not trust anyone other than the Crown Prince he had raised with his own hands.

"By the time you return, you will have grown up." Kangxi felt terrible inside.

Yinreng said, "Father Emperor, don't talk nonsense. I will still be a child when I return."

Kangxi was torn between laughter and tears: "By the time you return, Baoqing will have already moved out of the palace. How can you still be a child?"

Yinreng said, "What does my eldest brother moving out of the palace to establish his own manor have to do with me! I am still a child."

Kangxi personally straightened Yinreng's hair and clothes, his voice trembling: "Alright, alright, Baocheng is still a child. If you encounter anything on the way, come back immediately. Father only hopes that you and Baoqing return safely; nothing else matters, do you understand?"

Yinreng raised a smiling face: "Baocheng understands, and Eldest Brother understands too."

Yinzhi, standing behind Yinreng, nodded vigorously.

Kangxi placed the Crown Prince's headpiece on Yinreng, looked at him reluctantly for a long time, and then choked out, "Board the ship. Father will watch you leave."

After Yinreng and Yinzhi knelt and kowtowed to bid farewell to Kangxi, they boarded the large ship at the Tianjin port.

This scene was captured by both court painters and Western painters using their respective techniques and styles, becoming a landmark artifact of the turning point in modern Chinese history.

Songgotu and Mingzhu stood together, rarely not showing disdain for each other, both wearing expressions of worry, reluctance, and sorrow they could not suppress.

Songgotu choked up: "Your Highness the Crown Prince, this old servant kowtows to you. This old servant kowtows to see you off; you must return safely."

Mingzhu's voice trembled: "Stop kowtowing, stop it, it's unlucky. Which temple do you think is more efficacious?"

Tong Guogang had prayer beads strung all over his forearms, looking like a peddler of prayer beads. He was muttering something that sounded like unlucky words such as, "Don't you dare die out there, you must come back to die."

Other noble ministers whose children were accompanying them were also restless. They wouldn't even blink if they were injured on the battlefield, yet they were so frightened that their lips were trembling as their children boarded the ocean-going ship.

This could not be blamed on them.

The Manchus were a horse-riding people, meaning they were a land-based people. They had an instinctive, innate fear of the dark, vast ocean.

Even though this fleet would sail mostly along the coastline, they were terrified.

Unfamiliarity with the climate, pirate attacks, storms, underwater reefs... During this time, they had been frantically reading books related to sailing, and the more they read, the more afraid they became.

What they feared most was, how could the Emperor be so heartless?!

Previously, the Manchu nobles and clansmen had fought many battles with Kangxi over the position of the heir apparent, losing miserably, and had temporarily gone into hiding, waiting for other princes to grow up before making further plans.

In these power struggles, they were actually secretly impressed by the Crown Prince's intelligence and bearing; even with greed in their hearts, they admitted that this little Crown Prince was indeed almost perfect.

They also admitted that the Emperor and the Crown Prince had an exceptionally deep bond, and it was completely impossible to sow discord between them now.

They could only wait, wait until the Emperor was old, wait until the Crown Prince was mature, wait until an aging emperor felt jealous upon seeing the perfect grown-up Crown Prince, only then would it be possible to topple the Crown Prince.

But now, the Emperor had actually ordered his most beloved, perfect Crown Prince of the Great Qing to travel far to Europa?!

Does Your Majesty know how dangerous this is!

The Emperor must know. The Emperor had even sent the navy to Europa to participate in the war; how could he not know how dangerous the journey was!

Although they were jealous of Changtai, his status as a First-Class Duke and the Emperor's brother-in-law was clearly enough to represent the Great Qing in signing treaties with foreign nations! Why must the Crown Prince go?! What kind of immense benefit could there be that would make the Emperor willing to send the Crown Prince to take such risks??

It wasn't just the Crown Prince. The Emperor had sent out two princes who had just turned ten and had just grown up.

The nobles and clansmen often mocked the Crown Prince and the First Prince, saying there were already so many little princes in the palace, and these two wouldn't be arrogant for long.

But they never expected that after the Emperor had little princes, he would really let two grown-up princes take risks.

The mortality rate for children in this era was very high.

Three years old is a hurdle, six years old is a hurdle, ten years old is a hurdle, and every ten years after that is a hurdle.

Several little princes under the age of six combined were not as important as these two princes who had already passed the age of ten!

Not to mention that the Crown Prince was the perfect Crown Prince raised by the Emperor himself!

For the sake of the Great Qing's interests, could even the Crown Prince be put at risk?

Only a very small number of ministers in the court saw the importance of this negotiation; most of the court officials still held the mindset of the "Celestial Empire" and did not understand why Kangxi would let the Crown Prince take such a risk.

They only saw Kangxi's cold-bloodedness, and they only felt a deep chill.

"The Emperor still hopes for the Crown Prince to return; this ship full of noble children are all hostages."

There were others who said this.

They looked at these large ships as if they were looking at giant coffins.

Kangxi knew what some ignorant ministers thought of him.

He didn't care what those ignorant ministers thought of him.

When the large ships set sail, moving further and further away along the coastline, gradually turning into many dots, and eventually even the tops of the masts could no longer be seen, Kangxi felt empty inside, and his head buzzed, as if a piece of his heart had been hollowed out.

The Empress Dowager also came to the Tianjin port in person, standing on tiptoes to watch the Crown Prince sail away.

She stared blankly at the sea surface where the fleet could no longer be seen, motionless like a stone statue.

Fuquan and Changning exchanged a look and sighed in unison; one went to comfort Kangxi, and the other went to comfort the Empress Dowager.

Fuquan said, "Your Majesty, the Crown Prince and the First Prince have already set sail; you should return to the palace. It is windy here; if Your Majesty falls ill, how would His Highness the Crown Prince feel?"

Kangxi muttered, "Tell me, why am I so heartless to have agreed to let the Crown Prince go? How old is the Crown Prince? He just recovered from his illness."

Kangxi's hands trembled as he gestured a size: "He was especially frail when he was born, just this small. It was so hard for me to raise him up, and he was always getting sick, fainting, and couldn't stay in the palace for long."

"When he was little, he wouldn't sleep unless he was leaning against me. I have never seen such a delicate child."

"Every day he would complain that the palace was too desolate, and every few days he would want to go out of the palace to play. In winter, if he didn't go to soak in the hot springs, he would grab my sleeves and act spoiled, just like a pampered playboy."

"Every time I asked him to handle government affairs, he would complain endlessly, saying he was still a child, that he wanted to be a child for his whole life, that he hated trouble, hated being tired..."

As Kangxi gestured, his vision blurred, and he couldn't see clearly.

"I'm worried, I want to chase him back right now and tell him not to go. Changtai is overseas; leaving it to Changtai is enough. I shouldn't have let the Crown Prince go..."

As Kangxi spoke, he choked up and couldn't say another word.

"Your Majesty, let's return to the palace. We must all take care of our health and happily welcome Baocheng and Baoqing back." The Empress Dowager, crying, walked to Kangxi's side leaning on her cane.

This elderly grandmother gently pulled her grown grandson into her arms and patted his back, just as they had relied on each other when they were young.

"The Crown Prince and the First Prince will definitely return safely, bringing back great victory and glory. The Crown Prince is the child you and Fulin raised together; he is the heart's blood of two generations of Qing emperors after entering the pass, and he will absolutely not let the Great Qing or you down."

In the end, Kangxi and the Empress Dowager supported each other and boarded the carriage.

As they left, both Kangxi and the Empress Dowager lifted the carriage curtains and stared blankly once more in the direction where the fleet had disappeared.

In another carriage, Yinzhi sat with his feet tucked onto the seat, hugging his knees, silent.

The other younger brothers didn't quite understand what parting meant; they only felt the oppressive atmosphere in the carriage and kept their mouths shut, not daring to speak.

The carriage swayed gently, and Yinzhi's body swayed with it until he finally raised his head.

"Third Brother..." Little Yinzhen rarely had times when he couldn't speak, "Don't... eh?"

Little Yinzhen touched his face. He didn't know when, but his little face had already been wet with tears.

Yinzhi suppressed his sobbing voice: "Aren't you crying too?"

Little Yinzhen's mouth pouted, and he burst into loud sobs: "I want Crown Prince Brother! Crown Prince Brother is going for two or three years, is that true? Two or three years is too long! Crown Prince Brother has left Yinzhen behind again! Crown Prince Brother promised that he would definitely take Yinzhen on his next tour!"

Seeing that the two older brothers were crying, the remaining little princes, whether they understood the sadness or not, were all led into wailing.

...

"Hahahaha, I am now a Prince! A Prince!" Yinzhi held the imperial decree, his eyes squinting until they were invisible, "I haven't even moved out of the palace to establish my manor, and I've already obtained the title of Prince! From now on, call me Prince Zhi!"

Elundai held his sword and said, "Your Highness, why does this subordinate feel like this title sounds like the Emperor is scolding you?"

Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin covered their foreheads. This Elundai really dared to say anything!

Yinzhi wasn't angry; he laughed loudly and said, "Of course I know Father Emperor is scolding me. 'Zhi' (straight) means I am too straightforward and too reckless. But so what? He still granted me the title of Prince, hahahaha! I just hope to see Father Emperor look at me with displeasure while being unable to do anything about me!"

Yinreng, while gnawing on a fruit, said, "Eldest Brother, tone down your laughter; it's too arrogant. Although we won't return for two or three years, our words and actions on the ship will still be reported to Father Emperor."

Yinzhi said triumphantly, "Many things will happen in two or three years; they will only report major events. How could such a small matter be reported to Father Emperor? Hahaha, I am free!"

Yinreng, while gnawing on a fruit, had his mouth stretched wide.

That's right, I'm free!

Hahahaha, for these few years before returning to the capital, I can do whatever I want!

"Uncle said they set the negotiation time for the end of the year in December, which is our twelfth lunar month. We have plenty of time; we can stop for a day or two if we encounter prosperous ports along the way," Yinreng said with a smile, "but we shouldn't leave the ship to avoid getting sick from the change in environment."

What is the most feared thing about long-distance sailing? Storms? Pirates? Unfamiliarity with the environment?

The Great Qing's fleet was not crossing the Atlantic but sailing along the coastline; even if they encountered storms, they could return in time, so it wasn't dangerous.

After their fleet reached Taiwan, the navy stationed in Taiwan would escort them, and pirates would definitely turn and run upon seeing them.

Unfamiliarity with the environment was mainly a problem of bacteria and climate. They had brought enough medicine and famous Chinese and Western doctors, and they would not stay on shore for long periods before reaching Europe, so they were not afraid of it.

To prevent disease, Yinreng told the guards to wear masks when leaving the ship and to take a bath upon returning; all items on their bodies were either burned or scalded with boiling water and exposed to the sun.

Everyone on the ship that Yinreng and Yinzhi were on had to take a bath every two or three days; they had to wash their hands with soap before going to the toilet and eating.

Although Yinreng didn't quite understand the soap formula, they had soap. For hygiene, they used one ship specifically to store soap and clothing.

They also kept cats on the ship to prevent the plague.

Scientific prevention and sufficient medicine gave Yinreng confidence in dealing with diseases during the long voyage.

So what is the most feared thing about long-distance sailing? It's scurvy.

Yinzhi picked his ear: "Ah, scurvy? You've mentioned it many times before, and you're still mentioning it now? My ears are calloused from hearing it."

Yinreng slapped the table: "Because this is important, very important!"

Yinzhi said, "Yes, yes, yes, it's important, very important, so stop talking about it. If it gets out, our navy won't be able to win battles so easily."

Why was Changtai's navy invincible?

The Great Qing's ships and weapons were at most on par with Western maritime powers. Changtai's secret weapon was that the Great Qing navy's disease prevention measures were very well done. Especially scurvy; not a single person in the Great Qing navy contracted this "ocean killer."

It is now the 23rd year of Kangxi, which is 1684 AD.

In 1740, Vice Admiral George led two thousand people on an expedition, and only two hundred remained due to scurvy; in 1770, when the joint French and Spanish fleet attacked Britain, due to poor organization by the Spanish and a one-month delay after the French fleet assembled, two-thirds of the men died of scurvy...

During the Seven Years' War between Britain and France and the American Revolutionary War, most of the casualties in the long-distance navy were due to scurvy, not war casualties.

Changtai's long-distance navy could roam the ocean at will, and not a single crew member contracted scurvy. This combat effectiveness was at least 30% higher than that of other countries' navies.

As a long-distance army, how did Changtai contribute to the Franco-Dutch War? He just roamed the sea and occupied coastal ports.

Changtai drank tea on the ship and even set up dense wooden barrels on the deck to grow vegetables, watching the opposing navy chase behind their ship. As they chased, the crew members died in large numbers from scurvy.

How could the Great Qing fleet not be invincible?

Yinreng also planted vegetables on the deck.

The tradition of planting vegetables in wooden barrels on the deck began during the Song Dynasty.

Overseas trade was developed in the Song Dynasty. Although the crew members didn't understand scurvy, they were accustomed to planting vegetables in wooden barrels on the deck to be self-sufficient and improve their meals.

Long-distance sailing is boring; what else would you do if you didn't plant vegetables?

Because Yinreng had liked planting things in the Fengze Garden since he was a child, Yinzhi was also very used to helping his younger brother, the Crown Prince, plant things.

The two of them, one loosening the soil and the other watering, would spend most of the day after taking care of the vegetable seedlings.

Because both princes planted vegetables themselves, others on the ship also took up farming as a hobby outside of training and patrolling.

Chinese people have always regarded personally tending to flowers and plants as an elegant activity, unlike Westerners who think they are inferior if they get mud on their feet. Now they just turned beautiful flowers and plants into beautiful and edible vegetables.

Most of the noble children chose to plant vegetables that were relatively good-looking; some even brought tea trees on board and plucked tender leaves every day.

Only Elundai planted a large barrel of chives, harvesting one crop after another. Every day his mouth smelled of chives, which was particularly pungent.

The atmosphere of planting vegetables on the ship was strong, and the imperial physicians, having nothing to do, also asked for a few barrels to plant medicinal herbs.

Especially the Artemisia annua that Yinreng specifically named to be brought in large quantities; the imperial physicians planted several large barrels of it.

Many Artemisia herbs were also brought among the medicinal materials. For example, mugwort, which has broad-spectrum antibacterial effects in modern research.

In the future, Kangxi almost died of malaria, and quinine became the essential "miracle drug" in Qing dynasty time-travel novels. In fact, quinine has powerful side effects, and artemisinin is a better miracle drug for malaria than quinine. After traveling to the Qing dynasty, one should just find Artemisia annua for Kangxi to soak in water.

In ancient times, it didn't cure Kangxi because the malaria prescription used Artemisia argyi. The medicine that can truly cure malaria is recorded in Gui medicine, Dai medicine, and Tibetan medicine; it is not Artemisia argyi, but Artemisia annua.

Unfortunately, the imperial physicians only looked at Han Chinese prescriptions and did not believe in the medical prescriptions of ethnic minorities, otherwise, Kangxi would have been cured long ago.

Artemisia annua not only has artemisinin but also flavonoids. Flavonoids and their compounds are better specific drugs for scurvy than vitamin C; green tea polyphenols are flavonoid compounds.

Drinking tea every day might be a bit luxurious for ordinary soldiers, but everyone can afford to drink Artemisia annua water every day.

Yinreng and Yinzhi now drink a cup of Artemisia annua tea every morning. It is bitter enough to make them shiver and immediately wake up, which is more effective than strong tea.

The fleet brought several famous Western doctors.

These Western doctors were basically missionaries. Yinreng screened them and chose missionaries from countries hostile to France, such as Italy and Belgium.

Everyone on this ship basically spoke foreign languages. Kangxi asked Yinreng to bring this group of missionaries not only because he valued their medical skills but also because he wanted to use them for bargaining.

They also had their own calculations, hoping to contact the nobles of their motherland and mislead the Great Qing during the negotiations to seek benefits for their own countries.

Yinreng understood their calculations.

After the Kangxi dynasty defeated Tsarist Russia, they suffered a great loss in the "Treaty of Nerchinsk" because the Great Qing negotiation team, led by Songgotu, was tricked by missionaries.

In this lifetime of Yinreng, the Great Qing went to war with Tsarist Russia in advance and captured several restless missionaries, so the missionaries became much more behaved.

However, this group of people would not stop. In the original history, missionaries would even intervene in the "Nine Dragons Seizing the Heir" in Kangxi's later years. Yinreng was full of vigilance against them.

Therefore, Yinreng did not make the effects of Artemisia annua and tea public regarding scurvy, attributing it only to fresh food.

In fact, in this era, Europeans already knew that eating fresh vegetables and fruits could prevent scurvy. But because fresh vegetables and fruits were expensive during long voyages and the crew was lowly and easily replaceable, they not only did not promote it but also widely publicized that foreign fruits and vegetables were the culprits of scurvy.

Even by 1768, the British navy had suffered enough from scurvy, but they still suppressed the matter and asked experts from the Royal Academy of Sciences to issue a research report stating that "fresh vegetables and fruits, including lemon juice, are ineffective against scurvy."

It wasn't until 1780, after the British navy really couldn't afford to die anymore, that they admitted it and provided naval crew members with half a cup of lemon juice every day.

So Yinreng was not worried that after this group of missionaries knew that fresh vegetables and fruits could prevent scurvy, Western navies would provide fresh vegetables and fruits to the lowly, cheap, and easily replaceable sailors.

As for dried tea leaves and Artemisia annua, isn't that about the same as the pickled vegetables and dried vegetables that sailors eat? .jpg

The missionaries were arranged on the ship with Yinreng and Yinzhi.

Every day they would come out of the cabin and watch the nobles of the Great Qing leisurely planting vegetables on the deck, making the whole ship lush and green, looking like some scenic spot, and they were all amazed.

While amazed, this group of people also despised the nobles of the Great Qing, thinking that it was really improper for them to plant vegetables themselves.

The Han ministers accompanying them heard the missionaries whispering and all showed expressions of disdain.

The Han ministers did indeed despise this group of "mud-legged" nobles of the Great Qing in their hearts, but they despised them for many aspects, but they would definitely not despise planting vegetables.

Loving to tend to the fields is a manifestation of the Manchu nobles gradually becoming civilized after entering the pass.

From ancient times to the present, which scholar-official hasn't written one or two poems about their own farming? "Farming and reading family" has always been a synonym for elegance.

Even high-ranking noble families would open up one or two plots of land in their courtyards to farm themselves, as a way of feigning elegance.

Their ancestors had lived on this land for generations, and many of them had ancestral roots in the coastal regions.

If they were ruled by Westerners whose appearances were vastly different from Easterners, then judging by the way they treated other colonies, the very roots of their civilization would surely be dug up and destroyed.

When he discovered that the missionaries communicated using a special language, he had people eavesdrop and decode it. Finding out that these languages were their "dialects," he immediately set about learning them.

Chen Tingjing possessed an exceptional talent for languages; he had already mastered four or five dialects of a single foreign language.

There were no small number of Han officials like Chen Tingjing—after all, they were "ordinary parents to the people" who had once been able to chat heartily with local commoners anywhere across the empire.

Yinzhen almost laughed himself to death.

He thanked the Prince of Direct Descent on behalf of these missionaries in advance for immortalizing their names in history. This collection of missionary quotes would surely make a significant contribution to later generations studying this period of history.

A few days later, the Great Qing Imperial visiting fleet arrived in Taiwan and rested there for two days.

Yao Qisheng had been waiting at the Taiwan port for some time.

He had already successfully retired from office and moved to Taiwan to settle down, continuing to contribute his remaining energy to the mountains and rivers of the Great Qing. Although he currently held no official post, whether it was Changtai or Shi Lang, whenever they executed major decisions, they would go to seek Yao Qisheng's opinion.

"This old minister pays his respects to Your Royal Highness the Crown Prince and Your Royal Highness the Prince of Direct Descent," Yao Qisheng kowtowed.

Yinzhen helped Yao Qisheng up just as he was bending over.

He smiled and said, "This isn't our first time meeting, Lord Yao doesn't need to be so formal."

Yinti asked curiously, "Not the first time? You've met him before? Did you peep at him when he went to the Qianqing Palace?"

Yinzhen snapped back ungraciously, "I would never peep in the Qianqing Palace. When we were out on the streets playing, Lord Yao, Lord Huang, and General Shi were peeping at us from upstairs, and I saw them."

Yinti said, "Damn it! This old fellow actually does peeping too!"

Yao Qisheng: "..."

Shi Lang, standing behind Yao Qisheng: "..."

Yao Qisheng dryly laughed and said, "Did that happen?"

Shi Lang's expression distorted. Di-did that happen?

Yinzhen smiled and said, "Let's pretend it never happened. Although my eldest brother and I have done some homework, we have yet to make a long voyage. Do Lord Yao and General Shi have any reminders for us?"

Yao Qisheng hurriedly said, "Yes, yes, yes."

He pulled a huge book out from his bosom: "This old minister has written down every possible problem one might encounter during a long voyage."

Yinti was speechless: "Little brother, why does Lord Yao have the same hobby as you, pulling out a massive book of proposals anytime, anywhere?"

Yinzhen rubbed his nose and said, "Forewarned is forewarned."

He took the book handed over by Yao Qisheng and said, "When I return to the capital, I'll help Lord Yao publish it. Lord Yao will surely be hailed by later generations as a navigation expert."

Shi Lang muttered, "What kind of expert is he? That was clearly written by me."

He thought Yinzhen hadn't heard, but Yinzhen was sharp-eared and clear-eyed, and heard it very clearly.

Yinzhen held back a smile and said, "Of course, General Shi's name will also be listed as an author."

Shi Lang's dark face flushed red.

Yao Qisheng gave Shi Lang a look of deep disappointment, saying, "Pay no attention to him. Aside from knowing how to lead troops into battle, he knows nothing else."

Shi Lang muttered softly, "I know quite a lot..."

Yinzhen smiled at Yinti, "Brother, the way General Shi always likes to mutter softly in rebuttal is so much like you."

Yinti rolled his eyes: "I never mutter softly in rebuttal. I always rebut loudly."

Shi Lang: "..." How could his voice be so low, yet still be heard by the Crown Prince!

Shi Lang had originally wanted to leave a good impression on the Crown Prince and the Prince of Direct Descent. He had only muttered a couple of times—wouldn't that leave the Crown Prince with a bad impression?

In truth, having experienced years of frustration, Shi Lang wasn't usually so uninhibited when facing his superiors. However, after coming to Taiwan, Changtai was such a bold and unrestrained person, and they had become soulmates across generations, which gave Shi Lang a lot more courage.

Moreover, the atmosphere when chatting with Yinzhen and Yinti was very relaxed, and he was unconsciously drawn in by Yinzhen, finding it impossible to stay nervous.

Yao Qisheng was extremely exasperated.

He thought very highly of Shi Lang and his children. But Shi Lang's current performance... Oh well, he shouldn't blame Shi Lang; it was just that the Crown Prince was too formidable.

Some people could quickly dispel others' guard with their expressions and language, blending in with everyone. Even when occupying high positions, they made people unconsciously treat them on equal terms.

The Crown Prince was clearly such a person.

Although Shi Lang had initially felt he had spoken out of turn, once Yinzhen asked him a few questions and chatted with him about Taiwan and the navy, he had opened up completely, losing all the stiffness one usually felt facing the Crown Prince.

Yinzhen possessed extremely strong approachability. Meanwhile, the usually boisterous Yinti kept a straight face the whole time without joining the conversation, only occasionally chatting with Yinzhen when Yinzhen spoke, completely ignoring Shi Lang and fully displaying the arrogance of an imperial prince and a prince of the first rank.

After this meeting, Shi Lang said to Yao Qisheng, "Although Your Royal Highness the Crown Prince is approachable, His Highness the Prince of Direct Descent has an immensely strong aura. No wonder the Emperor wanted the Prince of Direct Descent to travel alongside the Crown Prince."

Yao Qisheng was speechless: "Is that all you managed to see?"

Shi Lang: "N-not enough?"

Yao Qisheng sighed: "No wonder you've wasted so many years in the capital. Your eye for people... Did you never think that the Crown Prince playing the good cop and the Prince of Direct Descent playing the bad cop was something they discussed beforehand? Did you not notice the high-ranking officials from the capital accompanying them—whose eyes held a more reverent gaze when looking at them?"

Shi Lang recalled for a moment and answered honestly: "Didn't notice."

Yao Qisheng: "..."

Shi Lang was quite old himself, but Yao Qisheng felt like brandishing the cane in his hand and beating Shi Lang just like a son.

Seeing Yao Qisheng so exasperated by him that he kept pounding the ground with his cane, Shi Lang smiled: "Though I didn't notice that, my judgment of people is still quite accurate. The Crown Prince's approachability is genuine, and the Prince of Direct Descent's arrogance is also genuine."

Yao Qisheng frowned: "Intuition?"

Shi Lang nodded: "Intuition."

Yao Qisheng fell into deep thought.

He had originally thought the Crown Prince was a deep and scheming person skilled at buying people's hearts, but a warrior's intuition like Shi Lang's was comparable to a wild animal's—it had never failed.

Shi Lang said, "When chatting with Your Royal Highness the Crown Prince, I was truly relaxed. I could feel that he genuinely treated me as an equal. I observed the Crown Prince with others; he even treats the little servants serving tea and water with a peaceful attitude. The Crown Prince's eyes hold everyone, whereas the Prince of Direct Descent's eyes hold no one except the Crown Prince and a few high-ranking officials and guards behind him."

Yao Qisheng murmured, "The Crown Prince's eyes hold everyone?"

Shi Lang nodded: "He looks at everyone, and everyone can enter his eyes. If you don't believe me, isn't the Crown Prince going out tomorrow to stroll down the busiest street in Taiwan Prefecture? Just observe."

Yao Qisheng nodded.

The next day, Yao Qisheng accompanied Yinzhen and Yinti—both traveling in disguise—onto the streets, paying close attention to Yinzhen's expression.

He was astonished to find that Yinzhen truly was, just as Shi Lang had said, a person whose eyes held everyone.

Let alone the Crown Prince, even ordinary aristocrats divided people by status and nobility when looking at them. Although their character and etiquette wouldn't let them deliberately look down on anyone, the education they received from childhood made them unconsciously ignore others.

For instance, small street vendors, tattered pedestrians walking by, accompanying servants... Even if their gazes fell upon these people, these individuals could not enter their eyes, as if they didn't exist at all.

The Crown Prince was different.

Whomever he looked at, that person's reflection would fall into his eyes.

When a servant handed him something, he would properly look back at the other person and reward them with a smile; when a vendor cried out their wares, he would curiously scrutinize their features, even being able to tell where they might have come from; when pedestrians brushed past them, he would considerately yield the way, and even pull the Prince of Direct Descent along to remark on how cute a particular child was.

Only then would the Prince of Direct Descent's gaze fall upon the pedestrian, his eyes mirroring that person's shadow, as he helplessly asked the Crown Prince if he was missing his younger brothers.

Yao Qisheng thought of the evaluation given to the Crown Prince by his brother-in-law Huang Xigun, who had fallen ill and returned home.

"The Imperial Crown Prince is as perfect as a sage."

A sage... Yao Qisheng smiled slightly and said to Yinzhen, "Taiwan has newly reclaimed a lot of farmland. Would the young master like to take a look?"

Yinzhen's eyes lit up: "I'd love to! What are you growing? Have high-yielding corn, potatoes, and sweet potatoes been planted? Taiwan has many mountainous areas; these crops should be vigorously promoted..."

Yinzhen's little mouth chattered away nonstop, causing Yinti to only rub his forehead.

"We're leaving soon, what farmland are you looking at? If you want to see it, linger in Taiwan for a few more days on your way back," Yinti said. "If you miss the negotiations, watch out for Emperor... Father skinning you when we get back."

Yinzhen said regretfully, "That's true. I'll just take a look at the farmland in the outskirts of the city. I want to see how they tend the fields. Big brother, don't you want to go take a look at the naval barracks?"

He attempted to persuade Yinti to stay one more day. Their time was plentiful; they didn't care about a day or two.

Yet Yinti crossed his arms over his chest to signal his refusal: "I only want to go to our uncle's camp early and see what a navy whose uncle won a great victory looks like. Don't even think about it, set off on time! I'm not going to haggle and bicker with so many ministers and generals just because of your wish to look at farmland—I hate trouble!"

Yinzhen slammed his face onto Yinti's shoulder: "Ouch! You're no longer the brother who loves me most."

Yinti said, "Right now, I'm the strict brother keeping a tight leash on a younger brother who runs wild like a wild horse with broken reins the moment he leaves the capital!"

Yinzhen let out another "ouch," feeling ever so wronged.

Watching this, Yao Qisheng couldn't help a smile of paternal warmth spreading across his face.

He finally understood why his brother-in-law had said, "When you see the Crown Prince and the Eldest Prince interacting, you'll know how rock-solid the Crown Prince's position is."

Look at the way the Crown Prince and the Eldest Prince interacted—it was even closer than ordinary brothers born of the same mother.

If the legitimate heir and the eldest born son of a concubine could get along like this, the Crown Prince's interactions with the other young princes in the palace were probably even more harmonious, and his prestige presumably even higher.

A struggle for the throne was truly impossible to occur.

"Your Royal Highness the Crown Prince should indeed prioritize the mission; this old minister was being presumptuous," Yao Qisheng said with a beaming smile. "I have prepared materials on Taiwan's arable land; Your Royal Highness can flip through them if you are bored."

Yinzhen instantly recovered to full health: "Great!"

Yinti rolled his eyes hard.

After Yinzhen had strolled around the city for a while, Shi Lang asked if Yinzhen had any feedback.

He had merely asked out of politeness, but Yinzhen pulled him aside and talked at length, laying out all the problems he had observed in the city.

Shi Lang gave a bitter smile: "For Your Royal Highness the Crown Prince to have noticed so many problems in such a short time, this subject feels deeply ashamed and unsettled."

Yinzhen smiled and said, "You've already done quite well, but if you want your name to be passed down in history, you can still work a bit harder."

In history, Shi Lang had practically treated Taiwan as his own private fiefdom, lording it over the region and cutting off communications between Taiwan and the mainland.

Yet several of Shi Lang's sons were officials on the mainland, renowned for their good governance and clean reputations, which proved that Shi Lang's education of his sons was actually quite good. His actions in Taiwan were probably an overcompensation for his family and clan.

Shi Lang had once been arrogant and reckless, and due to a misunderstanding, he had broken with Zheng Chenggong, resulting in the execution of his father and younger brother, after which the Shi family withered.

After defecting to the Great Qing, he was not given important responsibilities until his sideburns turned grey; it was only in his twilight years that he successfully attacked Taiwan and returned there.

Now aged, he used every means possible to amass wealth to provide for the Shi family members left behind in Beijing—this was a form of overcompensation.

Many corrupt officials had suffered displacement and hardship in their youth, with their families sacrificing greatly for them. Once they became officials, they would excessively compensate their relatives and clansmen.

Heshen, a capable and massive corrupt official of later generations, was also of this type.

Some people who had lived in poverty for most of their lives would empathize with the people's hardships after attaining high positions and become good officials; others, terrified by poverty, would frantically accumulate wealth to maintain their sense of security.

A classmate of Yinzhen's in his second life had once complained that after his family became wealthy, one parent refused to spend money and was obsessed with saving, while the other spent wildly and was obsessed with enjoyment, causing family friction. Yinzhen understood Shi Lang's mindset very well.

The officialdom of this Great Qing had no official who wasn't corrupt. Since they were all corrupt officials anyway, and Shi Lang's family was full of talent, Yinzhen hoped Shi Lang would restrain his greed and, even as a corrupt official, leave behind a somewhat better posthumous reputation.

Now Taiwan had Yao Qisheng and Changtai; it wasn't Shi Lang's sole domain. Although Shi Lang also seized some farmland, it was only to the extent that local officials typically did, not overly egregious.

Yinzhen could tell that Shi Lang's clothing and ornaments appeared very lavish. Although Shi Lang wasn't yet a mega-corrupt official, he was heading down that path. Therefore, he offered Shi Lang a subtle hint.

"To have one's name passed down in history..." Shi Lang chewed on these words with a mixture of emotions.

He had originally thought that by betraying Zheng and surrendering to Qing, wasting most of his life, even though he finally got his revenge, his reputation would likely remain ruined. All he could leave behind for his descendants was money.

"To have one's name passed down in history, eh." Shi Lang repeated it a few times, then suddenly burst into laughter: "What does Your Royal Highness want this subject to do?"

Yinzhen said, "Do what you ought to do, and train the navy well. The Great Qing is stepping out into the world, and naval generals are in short supply. There is already a military academy in the capital, and Imperial Father said a school should be built for the navy as well. If we don't build it now, we will have to build it in the future. In your spare time, you can write your military strategy into books."

Yinzhen earnestly said, "Military noble families are no longer in vogue, nor will the Great Qing allow any single family to monopolize an army or a region for generations. Why not emulate the great scholars, write books, establish doctrines, and open your doors to take in disciples? During the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, the influence of the School of Military Strategists was no weaker than that of the Confucians."

Shi Lang asked, "Does Your Royal Highness know about my son's affairs?"

Shi Shilun was a famous upright judge of the Qing Dynasty, written into operas, and his folk reputation was even higher than that of Yu Chenglong, the number one upright official of the Great Qing. Even into modern times, Beijing operas about Judge Shi were still being performed in major theaters.

A trace of awkwardness flashed across Shi Lang's eyes as he said, "Shi Shilun... he is quite ugly."

Yinzhen said, "Falling ill in childhood is not his fault. Being an official isn't about looks, and Imperial Father doesn't value—"

Before he could finish, Yinti interrupted: "Nonsense! Our Imperial Father pays special attention to a person's appearance. Shi Shilun can probably be a high-ranking regional official, but Imperial Father would never let him into Beijing to offend his eyes."

Kangxi didn't look at appearances? Just ask Cao Ziqing and Nalan Rongruo if they believed that!

Yinzhen was speechless: "Brother, could you stop tearing down my stage? Save some face for Imperial Father."

Yinti said, "Alright, alright, Imperial Father doesn't value outward appearance. Commander Shi, your son will definitely become a major regional official."

Shi Lang: "...Thank you." Should he be saying thank you?

When the son you left behind in Beijing as a hostage grows a bit older, I will propose to Imperial Father that he be admitted to Peking University. Speaking of that literary son of yours whom you delayed—Shi Shike—isn't he currently begging you to introduce him to Rongruo?"

Yinti sighed with emotion: "A person's reputation is like their shadow; Rongruo is simply the dream lover of all literati and poets in the Great Qing."

Yinzhen's face darkened: "Please refer to Rongruo as a role model respected by the literati of the Great Qing, or, to be more refined, as the silver moonlight spilling over the Mid-Autumn festival, as the fiery red plum blossoms amidst the white snow, as..."

Yinzhen said solemnly, "I am not joking."

Although Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin commanded the honor guard, they also held the concurrent post of imperial guards.

On the other hand, the two brothers Zhao Hongwei and Zhao Hongxi, sent by their father and Kangxi to act as bodyguards, had been dumped by Yinzhen and Yinti into the navy to undergo trials.

Military talent should look like military talent; let the bodyguards be handled by professionals.

——Mainly because Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin were good-looking. After growing out their bangs and shaving off their mustaches, they looked so handsome that Yinzhen and Yinti could eat an extra bowl of rice just looking at their faces.

Cao Yin held back a smile and said, "Rongruo, His Two Royal Highnesses are praising you; you should just graciously accept it."

Nalan Xingde rolled his eyes.

He and Cao Yin were very familiar with Yinzhen and Yinti; only when they were around could they dispense with protocol.

Originally Erlendai was supposed to be included, but he had fallen in love with eating chives and his mouth smelled entirely of them, prompting Yinti to chase him away with a scabbard. Now Erlendai was mingling among the mid-to-lower-level naval officers, arm-in-arm and completely integrated with them.

Shi Lang wore a complex expression. He didn't know whether he should be moved or terrified, and for a moment didn't know how to react.

Naturally, he should be moved that the Crown Prince remembered him; but the sons mentioned by the Crown Prince were all young, had not yet entered officialdom, and only served under him in the military—how did the Crown Prince know so much?

Yinzhen smiled at Shi Lang and said, "Changtai is my maternal uncle. His letters frequently praise your sons."

Shi Lang suddenly understood. He had forgotten that his soulmate, Grand Secretary Changtai, was the Crown Prince's own maternal uncle.

Shi Lang chuckled awkwardly: "Those unworthy sons of mine... compared to the Imperial Uncle, they are simply unmentionable."

Shi Lang's sons were roughly of the same age as Changtai. Shi Lang had originally thought he was very formidable, but after meeting Changtai, he couldn't help sighing that some military talents were born. (Changtai: Not born, taught by the Crown Prince.)

Yinzhen said, "My uncle is rather special."

Yinti asked in confusion, "What are you comparing anyone to uncle for? Uncle dares to fight with Imperial Father; do your sons dare?"

Yinti said, "Alright, it was sparring. After sparring, uncle even mocked Imperial Father for being weak."

Yinzhen took a deep breath: "No, no, don't listen to my brother's nonsense! Uncle respects Imperial Father very much!"

Yinti said, "He respects him, sure, but they still argue. Even when Imperial Father's snoring disturbed him, he would pick a fight over it."

Yinzhen: "...Big brother, shut up."

Yinti hurriedly covered his mouth.

Yinzhen smiled: "Imperial Father and uncle are close friends in private and occasionally sleep head-to-toe. It's completely normal for young people to scuffle."

Shi Lang: "..." How is he supposed to answer this?

So this soulmate Grand Imperial Uncle was this daring? He even beats the emperor? Even if that's your brother-in-law, you shouldn't fight with the emperor!

Changtai, who had clearly only been sparring—and had been dragged into sparring by Kangxi at that—suffered severe reputational damage.

Interrupted by his elder brother, Yinzhen dryly coughed a few times and changed the subject: "I have mentioned your sons' affairs to Imperial Father. You know General Zhao Liangdong, right?"

Shi Lang didn't know why the Crown Prince was asking about General Zhao, but among Han generals, Zhao Liangdong was basically the equivalent of Nalan Xingde among civil officials—a person's reputation was like their shadow, how could he not know?

"Of course. This subject regrets that when General Zhao entered the capital, I had already left it and missed the chance to chat with him," Shi Lang said. "General Zhao is currently the president of Peking University, right?"

Yinzhen nodded: "General Zhao is also my and my brother's martial arts master. Master Zhao's sons, Zhao Hongwei and Zhao Hongxi, are accompanying my brother and me on our visit to Europa this time. If General Shi is interested, I can also grant you two slots."

Shi Lang took a few deep breaths, immediately knelt, knocked his head, and said: "This subject's son Shi Shiji is adept at handling ordinary affairs and is meticulous; my son Shi Shipiao is skilled in military command and the most valorous. This subject requests that my two sons, Shi Shiji and Shi Shipiao, be allowed to attend by Your Royal Highness's side!"

Yinzhen said, "Granted."

After he helped Shi Lang up, Yinti asked curiously, "How do your two sons' combat skills compare to Master Zhao's two sons?"

Yinzhen: "..."

My instigating troublemaker of an older brother, he was practically one step away from waving his arms and shouting for them to start fighting right then and there.

116. Chapters 1 and 2 [V]

Zhao Hongwei and Zhao Hongxi kept a relatively low profile in the entourage. Most of the travelers were scions of nobility, and they wouldn't run around shouting whose sons they were. Naturally, Shi Lang had no idea of their identities.

Now that Yinzhi brought it up (fanning the flames), Shi Lang was also quite curious.

Shi Lang's son had followed him to conquer Taiwan, and Zhao Liangdong's son had also followed his father in suppressing the Revolt of the Three Feudatories. Both were young generals who had fought bloody battles.

Now, with young generals meeting young generals, their eyes...

Zhao Hongwei scratched his head: "Crown Prince, are we really fighting?"

Zhao Hongxi looked at his opponent's height. He wasn't really scared; it was just that if they actually fought to a winner, it would probably end in mutual destruction.

Yinzhen had people carry over a large pile of items: "Have a match; it can enhance understanding and build bonds. Not just the two of you, everyone come and have a match. Think of it as playing a game. Here is the rulebook, and here are the prizes."

Looking at the small notebook Yinzhen had produced, Yinzhi shrugged and sighed speechlessly.

His younger brother considered things so thoughtfully even just playing a game—he truly lived up to being his younger brother.

Rolling up his sleeves, Yinzhi also cheerfully joined the game.

Yinzhen didn't participate. If he went, these people wouldn't dare to let loose and play.

Strangely enough, while Prince Zhi was more arrogant and aloof, the imperial guards were actually more reserved around the Crown Prince.

Yinzhen brought out the skills of what later generations called the "Father of Games." His mini-games tested players' combat effectiveness while remaining full of fun, without hurting the opponents.

To hype it up so much, it was actually just ordinary fun competitive sports.

Cuju already existed in this era; Yinzhen introduced the rules of modern street football, which could test the players' reaction and athletic abilities;

Archery and shooting were mandatory training items in the military, to which he added fun target practice, such as shooting for prizes;

The navy had to fight in the water, so he designed a few competition events mimicking modern water variety show games...

After introducing all the games, Yinzhen clapped his hands and said, "The day before departure, play to your hearts' content! General Shi, you can also have the men in the army play these in the future. The dull military camp life ought to have some entertainment."

Shi Lang's hands were itching to play. After flattering Yinzhen a few times, he also joined the ranks of "playing."

Yao Qisheng was getting older, so he sat aside with Yinzhen to watch the battle.

Yao Qisheng said, "I heard that many novel games have emerged from the capital, combining education with entertainment and sweeping the Qing Dynasty. Some say they were made by the Crown Prince for his younger brothers, and this old subject originally thought it was just merchants talking nonsense."

Yinzhen smiled and said, "It is indeed merchant nonsense. Gu didn't only make games for his younger brothers."

Yao Qisheng was stunned, then laughed involuntarily: "Ah, right, there is also the elder brother. The Crown Prince certainly wouldn't leave Prince Zhi out of the games."

Yinzhen shook his head: "More than that. In the palace, the Grand Empress Dowager, the Empress Dowager, consorts, and princesses all love Gu's games."

Yao Qisheng asked, "Does the Emperor also love them very much?"

Yinzhen smiled and nodded: "The ministers like them quite a bit too. If Elder Yao wants them, Gu can have a set made for you as well."

Yao Qisheng immediately said, "This old subject is unworthy of such an honor!"

Yinzhen said, "Gu has already prepared it. With Big Brother keeping watch out there, shall we go inside for a chat?"

Realizing that what the Crown Prince wanted to discuss was definitely more than just games, Yao Qisheng immediately agreed.

Yinzhen and Yao Qisheng entered the room, where guards brought in a large box.

Yinzhen opened the box, took out a large sheet of paper, and spread it across the table.

Looking at the lines and outlines on the paper, Yao Qisheng felt a sense of familiarity, yet couldn't remember where he had seen them.

It wasn't until Yinzhen explained the meanings of the symbols on the map that Yao Qisheng exclaimed in shock, "A map of Taiwan?!"

He lunged over the table to inspect it closely for a long time, breathing heavily as he said, "This old subject has never seen such a detailed map before. Are these—are these mineral deposits real?"

Yinzhen said, "The terrain, minerals, vegetation, animals... they are all real."

Three hundred years later, Taiwan's topography remained unchanged.

Although liberal arts students couldn't save the world, they could draw maps.

Thanks to the Gaokao, and thanks to the cheat of treating his memory like a book he could flip through at any time, Yinzhen now possessed a rough distribution map of the world's terrain and natural resources in his head.

"These maps were obtained from the Dutch." Yinzhen shifted the blame to the Dutch colonists, "A peace treaty gift presented by their administrators."

Yao Qisheng's originally bloodless old face flushed red, his withered hair seeming to stand on end.

Gritting his teeth, his loose teeth practically grinding to pieces, he cursed, "Those red-haired wolves have wild ambitions! Utterly wild ambitions!"

Yinzhen said calmly, "Taiwan is merely their stepping stone. Zheng Chenggong was a hero, but unfortunately, the descendants of the Zheng family are utterly useless."

Zheng Keshuang, who surrendered to the Qing Dynasty, was only fifteen years old, and merely twelve when pushed into the position of a puppet—virtually a timid, weak, and indecisive child.

Kangxi originally wanted to confine all members of the Zheng family in the capital, and the future of the Zheng clan members would not be favorable.

Because the Zheng family's ancestral properties in mainland Qing had already been distributed to others when the Qing entered the Shanhai Pass; nor was it possible to return their lands in Taiwan. Trying to support a massive clan clearly stretched their resources to the limit.

Later on, this family scattered as commoners, disintegrating completely.

Respecting Zheng Chenggong as a hero, Yinzhen interceded for the Zheng family; Shi Lang also submitted a memorial—despite having a blood feud over the extermination of his family by the Zheng clan, he believed capable individuals among them could be employed.

In this lifetime, Kangxi was ambitious and extremely confident, not believing the Zheng family could cause him any trouble, so he did not keep them under heavy surveillance.

He disbanded and resettled the other branches of the Zheng clan. In the future, these Zheng family members could take the imperial examinations or join the military to gain official posts just like ordinary Qing citizens. The direct descendants of Zheng Keshuang remained in the capital, where Kangxi gave Zheng Keshuang the official post of an imperial guard and allowed him to enroll in university studies.

But how to put it—true to form for a group who tried to seize power through poisoning even as Qing warships sailed into their harbor, not a single one of them was fit for the grand stage.

Yinzhen could foresee that this direct lineage would probably end up living in poverty and destitution.

Among the clansmen willing to be dispersed, including Zheng Chenggong's youngest son, there were indeed a few talents Yinzhen thought highly of. Once these people settled down, they might rely on their own strength to enter the Qing officialdom.

"Since Zheng Keshuang has already surrendered to the Qing, the Qing will naturally acknowledge the Zheng family's achievements in resisting the Dutch," Yinzhen said. "This war waged by the Qing against the Dutch can also be considered China washing away the shame of Taiwan being occupied."

Knowing the court's disposition toward the Zheng family, Yao Qisheng sighed inwardly. The Emperor's boldness was growing stronger, and he was becoming more lenient toward the Han people; it was just a pity that no one in the Zheng family seized this opportunity.

Despite their opposing stances, Yao Qisheng also deeply admired Zheng Chenggong. Sadly, the Zheng family had no successors.

"This subject will develop the island as quickly as possible," Yao Qisheng said.

Yinzhen shook his head: "Taiwan has already returned; there is no need to rush. This map is for you to formulate long-term plans. Keep it for now, and let me talk to you about the development plans for Taiwan that are currently pressing."

Within a single day, Yao Qisheng had become completely devoted to this young Crown Prince, instantly adopting the posture of listening attentively.

Yinzhen's biggest concerns were: first, Taiwan was isolated overseas and difficult to manage; second, once the Qing navy witnessed the prosperity of maritime trade, they might turn to piracy.

He needed to find a legal way for the Qing navy to amass wealth.

Rivers had tribute transport, and the seas should also have fixed maritime shipping routes. These maritime routes could be escorted by the Qing navy in exchange for shipping fees.

This way, the navy could legally accumulate wealth while enhancing the connection between Taiwan and the mainland.

Letting the Qing navy engage in trade by imperial decree would certainly breed corruption, but for a feudal army, being able to conduct legitimate business was already quite good—definitely better than switching careers to become pirates. Since the Qing's maritime shipping routes were best run as state enterprises, incorporating them into the naval system was optimal.

The Qing Company already established by Kangxi would cooperate with the navy, allocating a portion of shares to them. In future business operations of the Qing Company, the navy would provide escorts and transport goods, earning a cut of the profits. This way, even without fighting wars, the navy would still have provisions and pay.

Viewed this way, the navy would certainly be wealthier than the army in the future, which would likely cause dissatisfaction among the land forces.

Then they would just have the navy make money and subsidize the army to improve the army's conditions.

Based on modern concepts and the current situation of various countries around the world, Yinzhen had already mapped out the future of the Qing Dynasty.

The Qing would not follow the old colonial path of territorial annexation; the Qing military budget could not sustain that. The path the Qing must take now was the new style of colonization that had already proved to be overwhelmingly profitable.

Territory could be bypassed; what they wanted were tangible benefits.

Lease ports, demarcate concessions, and strictly do legitimate business; fight wars as mercenaries and maintain friendly relations with all nations—a tariff reciprocity agreement alone would suffice...

Rather than calling it fighting a war, it was more like doing business. Every time the Qing navy went into battle, there had to be solid, practical benefits to reap.

Sustaining war through war was the most fundamental principle.

By doing this, the Qing could continuously reap benefits without arousing Western vigilance, while also earning a reputation for "benevolence."

In the Age of Discovery, where colonization meant pure plunder and slaughter, the Qing's approach was far too civilized, completely out of step with this world and this era.

"People in Europe would probably think we Qing people are stupidly kind," Yinzhen mocked himself.

After a long silence, Yao Qisheng bowed deeply toward Yinzhen: "The Emperor is benevolent, and the Crown Prince is benevolent."

Compared to kneeling and kowtowing, which symbolized the disparity between monarch and subject, a deep bow better demonstrated Yao Qisheng's admiration for the Emperor and the Crown Prince.

"Gu is not benevolent... Never mind, consider me benevolent then." Yinzhen let out a deep sigh.

In this era, practices that were clearly very cruel were actually considered benevolent.

Suddenly, Yinzhen felt a wave of exhaustion.

He forced himself to chat a bit longer with Yao Qisheng, telling him which regions of Taiwan were best for planting certain crops, and suggesting that Yao Qisheng set up offshore aquaculture along the coast to produce dried goods for the mainland market. After rambling on about a bunch of things, he finally went back to his room to sleep.

After Yinzhen fell soundly asleep, Yinzhi returned with a pile of prizes.

Ironically, these were prizes intended by the Crown Prince to reward the accompanying generals and ministers, yet they had all been won by Prince Zhi. The complexions of those who had participated in the competition were not looking very good.

They felt as though they had been heavily mocked by Prince Zhi.

"Why is Younger Brother so exhausted?" The moment Yinzhi saw Yinzhen's sleeping face, he knew Yinzhen had overexerted his energy.

He stormed off to question Yao Qisheng. Upon learning that Yinzhen had formulated a five-year and ten-year plan for Taiwan for him, he pounded the table in anger: "This lord can't take his eyes off him for even a second! That extraordinary ability of his is traded for with physical and mental strength! Just a tiny Taiwan, why does he need to go to such lengths?!"

Yinzhi was so angry that the prizes he had won lost all their appeal.

Yinzhen was always like this—desperately wanting to do everything he saw to perfection, even worse than Kangxi's perfectionism.

How did Zhuge Liang die? If his foolish younger brother inherited the throne in the future, wouldn't he work himself to death on the dragon throne?!

Terrified, Yao Qisheng asked, "His Royal Highness the Crown Prince—is His Royal Highness the Crown Prince ill?"

Taking a few deep breaths to calm down, Yinzhi replied, "He's not ill, just exhausted. He's too young; overdrawing his mental energy leads to extreme fatigue. Ordinary people calculate one step at a time, but he calculates five or ten years ahead—how could he not be tired?"

Hearing Prince Zhi point this out, Yao Qisheng finally realized how terrifying the five-year and ten-year plans given to him by the Crown Prince truly were.

What kind of person could foresee events five or ten years into the future? Zhuge Liang reborn?

He felt the plan in his hands burning hot.

"Don't let his hard work go to waste." Dropping these calm words, Yinzhi went off to find the kitchen to prepare some food.

He knew that when Yinzhen woke up, he would definitely complain about being starved flat and then devour twice his usual amount of food.

After Yinzhi left, Yao Qisheng immediately called a meeting with the various officials of Taiwan.

Looking at the map of Taiwan and its five- and ten-year plans, Shi Lang found it difficult to breathe: "Given by... His Royal Highness the Crown Prince?"

Sighing, Yao Qisheng said, "Yes, and it seems to have been done entirely by His Royal Highness the Crown Prince alone, consuming a great deal of mental energy. Prince Zhi flew into a massive rage at the Crown Prince because of it."

Through several walls, he had heard Prince Zhi's roaring.

Shi Lang stared at the plan, speechless for a long time.

......

By the time Yinzhen coaxed Yinzhi back into a good mood, it was time for them to set off again.

For this departure, Shi Lang dispatched the new-style warships to serve as the escort fleet for the Crown Prince and Prince Zhi.

Upon seeing this new-style warship, Yinzhen's jaw dropped wide enough to fit a fist.

A s-steamship?!

What the holy hell, am I seeing things?!

With his hands behind his back like an old man, Yinzhen circled the new warship and asked a barrage of questions.

Shi Lang had wanted to give Yinzhen a surprise, but he hadn't expected Yinzhen to know more about this warship than he did. He hurriedly fetched the craftsmen to answer Yinzhen's inquiries.

When Yinzhen and Kangxi toured the northeastern border, Yinzhen had proposed the idea of a steam engine. Kangxi had handed the idea over to the Ministry of Works, instructing them to gather craftsmen to research it.

Yinzhen's "whimsical ideas" had also been shared with Changtai, who was scouring for overseas master craftsmen in Taiwan to conduct research as well.

After researching for so long, they had actually managed to make some headway.

This steam engine had severe limitations. First, it was entirely handmade, making the manufacturing cost exorbitantly expensive; second, it was simply too large to be used on land vehicles; and third, its condensation cycle had major issues, and they couldn't find a cost-effective cooling method.

Therefore, such a bulky steam engine could currently only be used on waterborne vessels.

The current Qing steamships could carry very few sailors and weapons, lacking strong combat capability with a top speed only useful for running away—meaning ships this expensive that burned coal and could only be used for fleeing were utterly useless.

However, these few ships were currently just right to serve as escorts for the Qing Crown Prince's fleet.

Yinzhen and Yinzhi were not going out to fight wars. If Westerners lost their minds and tried to intercept them, all they needed to do was run away. The steamships could normally operate on human power, and when fleeing, they would start chugging along and burning coal, leaving intercepting fleets behind a trail of exhaust fumes—Yinzhen and Yinzhi would undoubtedly escape safely.

By the standards of this era's ship speeds, a steamship was a dimensional reduction strike.

"Study it well, and strive to replace all our Qing ships with steamships in the future." Yinzhen was so excited he was flustered.

Unable to calm down, he grabbed Yinzhi's hands and shook them vigorously.

Though still young, Yinzhi already possessed the indulgent and benevolent expression of an old grandfather.

Well, his younger brother acting all silly was truly cute.

"Alright, alright, leave it to them to continue researching. This is indeed a good thing," Yinzhi said, patting the iron contraption. "It would definitely be extra awesome to use as a pirate ship."

Shi Lang: "..."

Yao Qisheng: "..."

Calming down, Yinzhen said, "Indeed... Ah, whatever, forget it, we can't do that. Doesn't the Qing navy want any face?! But we could harass... No, no, no, let's not consider that for now. Let's first lower the cost and size, and strive for popularization."

Were steamships paddle steamers? Why were paddle steamers called paddle steamers? Was that "paddle" some kind of key component?

Yinzhen shook his head hard, but unfortunately, nothing shook out.

He only remembered that all modern ship engines used propellers; perhaps he could have the craftsmen try researching propellers?

Yinzhen faintly remembered the appearance of a propeller. Even if he couldn't remember, the word "propeller" might make the craftsmen think of something.

Actually, Yinzhen's direction of memory was completely wrong.

Paddle steamers were called paddle steamers because early steamships were propelled by paddle wheel propulsion.

Paddle wheel ships had already existed during the Song Dynasty, but because paddle wheels were too bulky and difficult to turn, they were quickly phased out. It wasn't until the advent of the steam engine that paddle wheels were brought back into use.

But even with steam engine propulsion, the shortcomings of paddle wheels remained obvious. Later, paddle wheel propulsion was improved into propeller propulsion, and subsequent steamers were all propelled by screws, merely retaining the term "paddle steamer" (lunxuan) in translation or custom.

By a fluke, Yinzhen had bypassed "paddle steamers" and directed the Qing craftsmen's research straight to "propeller-driven ships."

Unfortunately, Yinzhen kept hoping to leap from steam engines to internal combustion engines, but the craftsmen's research had stalled at the ignition stage and made no progress.

The liberal arts student Yinzhen was completely oblivious to the fact that internal combustion engine ignition required electricity, and he hadn't even developed electricity yet.

With a trace of regret, Yinzhen embarked on a new journey aboard the ugly steamship.

Every now and then, he would go tour the steamship, and even filled it with vegetable patches, bringing a fond, gentle smile to the accompanying guards.

Why was their Qing Crown Prince so adorable? It really made one reluctant to let foreigners catch a glimpse of their little Crown Prince.

Unable to stand it anymore, Yinzhi dragged Yinzhen away: "Enough, enough, stop touching it. Haven't you touched it enough yet?! Don't waste your time stroking a boat! Can you go do some real work?"

Yinzhen said, "Alright, alright, real work, real work. Let's draw maps!"

Tilting his head in simple-minded confusion, Yinzhi asked, "Huh?"

He found that he was starting to fall behind his younger brother's train of thought.

No, he had probably never kept up with it in the first place!

When Yinzhen spoke of drawing maps, he meant drawing a distribution map of the surrounding national powers of the Qing Dynasty.

This was already the era of great navigation and great colonization; Southeast Asia had almost entirely been colonized. In other words, the Qing Dynasty was already surrounded by colonists.

Changtai had discovered this problem when he started leading the navy to roam around. But without satellite maps, it was difficult for him to draw an intuitive distribution map of powers.

This was no problem for Yinzhen.

He already had a detailed map in his mind; all he needed to do was ask local noble clans, bribe local officials, and fill in the names of the colonizing nations.

Setting off south from Taiwan, the Qing imperial delegation made another port call in Cambodia to resupply.

Yinzhen requested this stop because they were about to pass through the Strait of Malacca, which was currently under Dutch control, and the Qing and the Netherlands were still enemy nations.

Cambodia had won the Cambodian–Dutch War in 1644 and expelled the Dutch colonists. Afterwards, the Cambodian king who drove out the colonists was backstabbed by domestic Buddhists, turning Cambodia into a vassal state of Vietnam, while the Qing was the suzerain state of Vietnam. Without needing any rounding, Cambodia could nominally be considered part of the Qing's sphere of influence.

Unfortunately, they were currently in the middle of Cambodia's brief war of resistance against Vietnam. A few years prior, King Chey Chettha IV of Cambodia had just defeated the Vietnamese army; now, Vietnam was supporting Ang Non, the usurper whom Chey Chettha IV had driven from the throne, in fighting against Cambodia. As Vietnam's suzerain state, without needing any rounding, the Qing was currently considered an enemy state by Cambodia.

When the Qing delegation docked at the Cambodian port, Chey Chettha IV was so frightened he rolled right off his throne.

Minister: "Your Majesty! Should we expel the Qing people?"

Crawling up from the floor, Chey Chettha IV kicked the minister over: "Expel my ass! Prepare a carriage—no, prepare a horse! This king will ride at breakneck speed to personally welcome the Crown Prince of the Qing!"

Author's Notes:

A brief popular science on the distribution of South Asian forces during this period:

1. Vietnam was divided into north and south, with the Qing as its suzerain state. At this time, Vietnam wasn't called Vietnam yet, but for the readers' convenience, it is referred to as Vietnam;

2. Cambodia drove out the Dutch and was then controlled by Vietnam, but the Crown Prince's visit coincided with Cambodia's brief period of resistance;

3. Malacca was controlled by the Dutch;

4. The Philippines were controlled by Spain.

117.三更（16w营养液加更） [V]
吉·哲塔四世气喘吁吁赶到港口的时候，大清已经安营扎寨，生火做饭。
大帐一立起，大清的驻扎地，居然比柬埔寨的小城市更显繁华。
吉·哲塔四世来到大清营寨前，居然不敢上前。
梁九功此次也幸运地一同出行。
他换上了特别定做的内侍服装，背在胤礽的要求下挺得笔直，腰间也配着刀，看上去仿佛寻常习武的富贵公子。
胤礽猜测柬埔寨会派人来，让梁九功领着人早早等候。
之所以不让其他侍卫和大臣等着，是因为梁九功身份特殊，来人无论地位如何，他接待都算合适；而且梁九功更擅长观察，能在对方前来的第一时间就拿出合适的态度应对。
柬埔寨也是说汉语。梁九功一见到吉·哲塔四世，就从周围人对他的称呼中得知了他的身份。
他笑眯眯地用接待藩王的礼仪接待了吉·哲塔四世一行人，然后将其安排到一处帐篷，遣人给这群人打理卫生。
吉·哲塔四世晕乎乎地被一群内侍簇拥进一个帐篷洗澡换衣服，直到摸到自己身上的藩王服装时才惊出了一身冷汗。
他居然这么松懈！如果大清对他有敌意，他怎么死的都不知道！
不过……
吉·哲塔四世理了理衣服，悲哀地想，大清大概不会把他放在眼里，大清的太子才不会暗杀他呢。
谁都知道华夏是礼仪之邦，原本吉·哲塔四世听到华夏换了一个野蛮人当主人，还以为华夏已经变野蛮了。
现在大清的做派让吉·哲塔四世发现，华夏还是那个华夏，只是换了个国王……换了个皇帝，内在一点改变都没有。
大清根本没有表现出任何傲慢，接待他的人也彬彬有礼，但是吉·哲塔四世却发现自己似乎处处低人一等，连别人温和的态度，似乎都是对自己轻视。
吉·哲塔四世身边的重臣也是这样的感受。
他们看着那些衣着华丽，举止优雅的大清人，神情恍然。
柬埔寨的君臣见过许多强国的人。
后黎（即越南）的阮氏也好，荷兰人也好，葡萄牙人也好，西班牙人也好，他们强大高傲不可一世，却从未给柬埔寨的君臣们这么大的心理压力。
大清人明明对他们和蔼可亲，招待十分周到，他们却像是被什么庞然大物注视着，内心不由蜷缩，整个灵魂都在颤抖。
胤礽坐在最上首。胤禔也坐在上首处，椅子稍稍倾斜，视觉上呈现出坐在胤礽左下侧的效果。
其余文臣武将分左右依次座位排开，中间空出一片地。
胤礽打量了愣着不敢动弹的柬埔寨君臣们一会儿，心中了然。
五千年的文明礼仪压制，让这群人脑袋一片空白了啊。
这就像是乡下人第一次进城，看着高大的建筑和衣着时尚的人，忍不住缩着脑袋弓着背不敢看人似的，自惭形秽了。
陈廷敬不满地训斥道：“柬埔寨国主见我国太子、直亲王，为何不拜？！”
明明现在已经在反抗越南，不能算是大清藩王下臣的吉·哲塔四世一个激灵，纳头就拜：“本王、不不不，小王吉·哲塔四世，叩见上国太子！叩见上国亲王！”
胤礽微笑着伸出一只手：“请起，赐座。”
梁九功指挥着内侍搬来椅子，吉·哲塔四世颤颤巍巍地坐在椅子上，只敢坐半个屁股。
胤礽道：“你们反抗安南，是要独立于大清？”
吉·哲塔四世腿一软，从椅子上滑到了地上，磕头道：“小王不敢！小王愿独立为上国纳贡称臣。”
胤礽点头：“那就是不想附属于安南，想直接向大清臣服？”
吉·哲塔四世心里咯噔一下，没想到自己脑子一抽，居然会说出这种话，一时不愿回答。
胤禔冷哼一声：“太子问你话，你要犯上？”
吉·哲塔四世身后一个重臣不满道：“本国本就未臣服大清，乃是大清平等国家，你们……”
“闭嘴！”吉·哲塔四世训斥道，不断磕头道，“不要听他胡说，小王愿意臣服，愿意臣服！”
那重臣眼中闪过不满，正想再说什么，鄂伦岱一拍椅子：“忤逆太子，捆起来，押外面掌嘴。”
侍卫立刻将那重臣制服堵嘴拖走。
柬埔寨的君臣看到这一幕，居然不敢动作。
胤礽叹气：“那人应该是安南的奸细。安南看来对大清也不是很忠诚了。”
胤禔好奇：“弟弟，你怎么知道？”
胤礽道：“现在柬埔寨国王在大清军营中，若得罪孤，或许会有杀身之祸。他却故意激怒孤，大概是想用他那条命，把柬埔寨国王留在大清军营，借刀杀人吧。”
胤禔“哦”了一声，道：“那柬埔寨国王挺惨。我们把他杀了就杀了，柬埔寨一点办法也没有。”
吉·哲塔四世：“……”
柬埔寨重臣：“……”
“起身吧，大清不是霸道的国家。”胤礽再次伸出手往上抬了抬，“以前大清着眼国内，没有余力为你们梳理关系。如今大清内部已经安顿，海军已经可以腾出手保护你们。以后大清会致力于恢复南洋海上贸易，让诸藩国都能享受到天.朝上国的荣光。”
胤礽轻拍了一下手，内侍将吉·哲塔四世扶起，并在吉·哲塔四世面前放了一张矮桌。
又一个内侍走出，捧出一卷文书，放在吉·哲塔四世面前。
吉·哲塔四世不敢打开文书，生怕看到自己不愿意看的东西。
胤礽微笑：“这些年大清处理国内的事花费了些功夫，如今北方的罗斯国已经求和赔款，南方的台湾郑家已经降服，曾骚扰大清海岸的荷兰首都被大清的盟军攻克……”
吉·哲塔四世声音颤抖：“荷兰被大清攻占了？！马六甲的荷兰？！”
陈廷敬忍不了了。
他站起来，训斥道：“放肆！太子殿下还未说完话，你插什么嘴！”
胤禔不耐烦地挥挥手：“罢了，陈师傅坐下。你能指望乡下小国懂什么礼仪？这曾经是安南的藩国，安南又是大清的藩国，他们是藩国的藩国，能会说汉话就不错了。”
被胤禔安抚后，陈廷敬躬身行礼后，用眼刀子剜了吉·哲塔四世一下，才拂袖坐下。
胤禔没好气道：“荷兰霸占了台湾的事虽发生在前明，但台湾是我中国领土，中国朝代如何更替是我们自己的事，红毛番人胆敢出手，就要承担我们的怒火。如今太子和本王就是要前往欧罗巴，和荷兰签订停战赔款协议。”
《论语》曰，“诸夏，中国也”。“中国”在华夏历史上是一个地域概念，凡是大一统的中原王朝，皆称中国。
因所有王朝都把历代王朝当做自己历史的一部分，所以包括大清在内，对外自称中常将“中国”和自己国名混用。
历史上的《尼布楚条约》，大清的自称就是“中国”。
现在大清使团出访外国，为彰显大清的底蕴，对外也是称“中国”——我们只是换了皇帝，但国家未变。
胤禔停顿了一会儿，给这闭目塞耳不知世界局势的藩国的藩国国主一些消化这段信息的时间，然后道：“从古至今，中国和周围藩国都是一荣俱荣，大清将分享荣光与诸国，你还不跪谢大清隆恩？”
吉·哲塔四世眼露绝望。
他知道，他就知道。天.朝上国一统之后，周围哪有别人置喙的余地？
柬埔寨的历史书中一直描写着隔壁天.朝上国的可怕。其他大臣或许只看到衰落的大明，无法理解天.朝上国的恐怖，但身为国王他很明白，一旦这庞然大物结束了内乱，缓过了气，开始注视着周围，这四方天地皆是天.朝上国的领土。
吉·哲塔四世眼露绝望，手指颤抖，翻开文书。
当他看完文书第一页之后，不敢置信地抬头，然后立刻垂下头几乎飞快翻看文书，眼睛越来越亮，心情越来越飞扬。
大清文书说，藩国自治，大清从不干涉别国国政，就算你们换皇帝，只要承认大清是宗主国，我们都不管；
大清文书说，大清不要领土，只租借一些港口作为大清海商和海军驻扎地，海军会保护藩国不受西方殖民者欺负；
大清文书说，大清不收税，每年只需要纳一些珍惜物品作为供奉就行，大清还会恩赐更好的东西，双方只需要免除边关关税，就算宗主国和藩国一体……
吉·哲塔四世看完之后，脑袋里满是不敢置信。
大清、大清这是来做慈善？
史书中记载的天.朝上国全是冤大头居然是真的！
