128. First and Second Update [V]

Yinreng regretted it.

Yinreng truly regretted it.

Seeing the circle of people around him, Yinreng regretted it more than he could possibly express.

He began to recall how he had ended up in this situation.

Oh, he had started interviewing. The interviews were very successful. To appease their anxiety about heading to an unknown country, he had engaged in pleasant academic exchanges with them.

Then, his good older brother, the Prince Zhixin, flicked his sleeves and left him alone among this group to talk about numbers, physics, and chemistry, while he went off to hunt.

Yinreng looked up at the eager, enthusiastic, and worshipful gazes of those around him, then looked down at the formulas and theorems on the paper in front of him; his head felt like a balloon being inflated, gradually expanding.

I’m a liberal arts student who didn't even study advanced mathematics in college; why am I here discussing math, physics, chemistry, and biology with foreigners?

And I’m discussing it in a foreign language!

Spoken foreign language and professional foreign language are two different things, okay! My foreign vocabulary is nowhere near enough to let me understand their theories!

What? They want to write it out with numbers and draw it out with diagrams? Oh, that’s fine then.

Fine, my foot! I don't want to discuss these things with you at all! And even if I see the calculations and diagrams, I don't understand them!

Heavens, as a liberal arts student, how did I end up here?

You might ask, as the Crown Prince, if you don't want to talk, you don't have to.

But Yinreng is not an ordinary Crown Prince; he is a transmigrator with a very deep sense of responsibility.

This group of people all claimed they had found inspiration and that if they could just trouble Yinreng for a little bit longer, they could derive the formulas and theorems.

Yinreng really couldn't bring himself to say, "Let's talk about it tomorrow."

When Leibniz heard that Yinreng was holding an academic seminar (?), he ignored his own agitated state, clutched a pile of draft paper, and squeezed his way over.

Count me in!

Textbooks occasionally had derivation processes, so Yinreng could barely provide them with some inspiration. But he was limited to providing inspiration; he couldn't do anything else.

Yet, for some reason, even if he said a load of nonsense, the other party would excitedly say, "I have realized it!"

Realized what? I don't understand! I was just encouraging you!

Yinreng maintained a stiff but polite smile, cheering each of them on.

Soldiers and attendants kept handing over paper and ink, replacing the worn-out quill pens.

Under Yinreng’s gentle gaze, this chaotic group consciously lined up.

Before Yinreng arrived, while they were researching together, they had already "decided" who was the best in each discipline.

These top experts surrounded Yinreng, while others did their calculations a bit further away. Whenever they had a new discovery or question, they would line up in front of Yinreng, asking for guidance from him and the experts by his side.

In front of them were delicious tea and pastries—although the tea lacked sugar and milk, after drinking it for a while, they found that such bland, clear tea had a unique flavor, becoming more pleasant the more they drank.

When they needed to use the restroom, they would leave quietly and return just as quietly.

They whispered to each other, their eyes filled with the light of wisdom and ambition.

How did what was supposed to be a simple "interview" turn into a brainstorming session where almost everyone had a flash of inspiration?

Yinreng didn't know; Yinreng really didn't know.

He could only blankly maintain his smile, saying things he wasn't even sure were correct, and then curse silently in his heart when the other person claimed they had "realized" it.

Realized my foot! Why haven't I realized anything!

How exactly did things develop to this point?

When Yinreng went to sleep, he still hadn't figured it out.

The next day, seeing them gathered together again, he couldn't help but feel a string of ellipses in his heart.

Yinzhi: "Do you want to come hunting with me, or continue to suffer?"

Yinreng looked at the eager eyes of that group, his expression stiff, his tone dejected: "I, I..."

A group of foreign researchers: Starry-eyed.jpg.

Yinreng said dejectedly: "Big Brother, just knock me out and drag me away."

Yinzhi patted Yinreng on the shoulder: "Little brother, I'm going hunting, see you later."

After saying this, the Prince Zhixin flicked his sleeves and left again, leaving behind his poor Crown Prince brother.

Yinreng looked back three times as he went into the pile of foreigners, then revealed a fragile, exhausted, yet still gentle smile: "Let's continue."

Foreign researchers: Cheering.jpg!

Yinreng sniffled and decided to hate his big brother for half a day.

And so, poor Yinreng spent five days recuperating in the estate, all five days spent with this group. Even worse, a group of unwilling-to-be-outdone Han and Manchu officials joined in.

Who doesn't know arithmetic! I want to see just how good you Westerners really are!

Seeing this group of Han and Manchu officials quickly learn the new numbers and mathematical expressions, Yinreng was full of question marks.

Could it be that I am the only useless one among all these people?

Cupping his hands, excuse me!

Westerners had a strong body odor; even though this group had been arranged to bathe properly, as soon as they got excited, there was still a sweaty smell. Yinreng felt like he was being fumigated.

However, these Westerners believed that Yinreng brought his own air-freshening effect, and the scent around him was particularly pleasant.

This Great Qing Crown Prince might truly be a Son of God with a self-purifying effect.

He was knowledgeable but refused to take any credit. When everyone said they wanted to thank Yinreng in their papers, Yinreng refused them all, saying not to include his name.

Yinreng said nobly: "I am only telling you the thoughts of the ancient Chinese sages, not my own thoughts."

Enough! I’m a liberal arts student; I don't want to be called a mathematician, physicist, chemist, or biologist by future generations! I won't have peace even after I die!

Just thinking about his portrait and name being printed in math, physics, chemistry, and biology textbooks made Yinreng start to tremble! I hate math, physics, chemistry, and biology! I’m allergic to them!

This group had no choice but to obey the Crown Prince's orders.

Almost all of them later went down in history, leaving behind numerous papers and works. In their famous works, they would always thank a mysterious, unmentionable person.

Thus, Yinreng became the "you-know-who" in the mouths of future science students; it was quite prestigious, just like that person with no nose.

After Ms. Rowling's noseless character was put on the big screen, Yinreng's portrait was grafted onto the noseless one by science students who "hated" him, singing songs about math, physics, chemistry, and biology terms with synthesized voices, becoming the "Ghost-Animal Emperor" of the new era.

Yinreng didn't know any of this now, and he never wanted to know.

He only knew that he had previously liked the treacherous world of fame and fortune, hypocritically flattering nobles from various countries.

It turned out he loved the troublesome business of noble socializing and political negotiation! He really liked it!

"Finally able to get rid of them." Yinreng rubbed his face hard with both hands, twisting it into all sorts of strange shapes.

He was going crazy!

Yinzhi said huffily: "If you want to refuse, you can refuse immediately. If you don't refuse yourself, who are you blaming?"

Yinreng pounded Yinzhi: "Can I refuse? They said they were about to have an inspiration! I can't refuse!"

Yinzhi opened his arms and nimbly caught Yinreng’s rain of punches: "That’s your own problem. You think their inspiration is important, so you indulge them. But thanks to you, not only are they coming to the Great Qing with us, but they are also writing to friends to bring even more people to the Great Qing. Maybe having you is more efficient than Uncle kidnapping people."

Yinreng punched for a long time, but not a single blow landed on Yinzhi, leaving him panting for breath.

He leaned against Yinzhi: "As long as they can persuade more people to come to the Great Qing, I can die without regrets."

"Don't talk about dying, it's unlucky." Yinzhi helped tidy up Yinreng’s disheveled clothes. "I heard Louis XIV is an emperor as capable as our Imperial Father. Do you have confidence?"

The Western leaders currently involved in this Dutch War—which didn't exist in history—were all gathered in the Dutch capital. Yinreng first had to meet with Louis XIV in private to discuss the division of spoils.

France also tried to get involved in Nanyang (the South Seas); Yinreng and Louis XIV’s private meeting had to resolve the Nanyang issue first before discussing anything else.

Louis XIV was also a pious and fanatical Catholic; he might propose that the Great Qing promote Catholicism.

The burden on Yinreng’s shoulders was very heavy.

Yinreng said: "Negotiation is not just about who has more cards, but about adapting to circumstances. What confidence do I have? At worst, we just break it off."

Yinreng clapped his hands and spread them.

"We are far away from France, and there are no conflicts of interest at the moment. Do you understand 'ally with the distant, attack the near'?" Yinreng said, "I think Louis XIV, as the Sun King, wouldn't fail to understand that."

After Yinzhi finished tidying Yinreng’s clothes, he patted Yinreng’s back, telling him to sit up straight: "I hope he understands, otherwise French ships won't be entering Nanyang again."

Yinreng nodded.

When the Great Qing motorcade arrived at the estate where Louis XIV was staying, the attendants got off first and laid a layer of silk in front of the Crown Prince and Prince Zhixin’s carriage.

Silk?!

Louis XIV, who was standing at the door to welcome them, felt his eyelids twitch fiercely.

Although they would lay carpets on the ground, this was silk!

No, no, no, he couldn't think like that. In the ancient Eastern country, silk was just like an ordinary carpet. That must be it.

Bolt after bolt of silk was moved off the carriage and laid out in front of the carriage, all the way to the entrance of the estate.

A eunuch bowed in front of the carriage door. Changtai, who was leading the way on horseback, dismounted, walked to the carriage, and lifted the curtain.

Yinreng, wearing a ceremonial dress modified to better show off his figure, held Changtai’s hand, stepped on the eunuch’s back, and stepped off the carriage.

Yinzhi followed closely behind.

The Imperial Guard, led by Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin, dismounted, held their flags, gripped their swords, and formed a formation.

On the ship, Yinreng had properly trained this group of guards in their demeanor and movements, modified their clothes, and unified their hairstyles.

Now their hairstyles were uniform short hair in the front and a small braid in the back, topped with Great Qing official hats, carrying a unique, untamed Manchu wildness within their meticulous appearance.

Coupled with their deliberately tightened waists and straight trouser legs, it made the noblewomen’s eyes shine.

Yinreng walked with a steady, upright gait to the stunned Louis XIV, smiled, bowed, and nodded: "Great Qing Crown Prince Aisin Gioro Yinreng. It is an honor to meet His Majesty Louis XIV, Emperor of France."

He used the etiquette of a Great Qing junior to a senior, neither humble nor arrogant.

Louis XIV recovered from the spectacle of the Great Qing Crown Prince and hurriedly supported Yinreng: "The Great Qing Crown Prince’s French is very good."

Yinreng said modestly: "To serve as an envoy, one must naturally practice foreign languages well. Thank you for the compliment, Your Majesty."

Louis XIV laughed loudly: "I have long admired the Great Qing Emperor in spirit; if you don't mind, you can call me uncle."

Yinreng said: "Imperial Father said that Your Majesty is his friend, so you are naturally my uncle. Uncle can call me Yinreng directly."

Louis XIV tried to imitate the sound of "Yinreng," which was a bit of a tongue-twister, but after trying a few more times, he could barely pronounce it.

Yinreng then introduced his older brother, Prince Zhixin Yinzhi, to Louis XIV.

Louis XIV looked at Yinzhi very seriously.

He had already received news that it was this Prince Zhixin who had completely uprooted the Dutch influence in Nanyang.

Because Yinreng had arranged his life since childhood, Yinzhi had sufficient protein intake and was often in the sun, so he was quite tall; although he was only twelve, he was already over 1.65 meters.

Yinreng’s height was also over 1.6 meters.

This height was nothing among their peers in later generations, but in this era, it was already taller than many adults.

For example, the former heir of the Guangnan Kingdom, who had once mocked Yinreng for being childish, was almost terrified when Yinreng stood up. Because he claimed to be a strong man, but was actually only 1.5 meters tall.

A fun fact: although later generations boast about how tall Europeans are, before the Industrial Revolution, i.e., the 19th century, the average height in China was actually consistently at the forefront of the world, and the average height of northern Chinese people was not much different from the "giant country" of Northern Europe.

According to 18th-century conscription reports, the Norwegian conscription requirement for male height fluctuated between 1.6 and 1.65 meters, indicating that their average male height was definitely below 1.6 meters.

In ancient Chinese tombs, it can be seen that the height of buried male commoners was basically above 1.6 meters, while the height of male owners of noble tombs in the Western Han Dynasty was basically over 1.7 meters.

It wasn't until the Industrial Revolution that the height of Europeans surged, leaving China far behind.

Therefore, Yinreng and Yinzhi’s current heights, even among European nobles, were considered tall and heroic.

Even though they were young, noblewomen had already begun to tidy their appearance, showing their most beautiful smiles to Yinreng and Yinzhi.

They were young, but we don't mind!

Yinzhi minded very much. He used his body, which was a size larger than Yinreng’s, to block those people’s unreasonable gazes, and glared at the group of noblewomen.

Yinzhi said huffily: "The etiquette between China and the West is truly very different. My brother, as the Crown Prince, has never been looked at so unscrupulously by anyone other than family. However, these people are relatives of the French Emperor, and my brother is just a Crown Prince, so let them look. Their status should be high enough to look at the Crown Prince, right?"

Yinzhi lifted his chin: "Are they princes, princesses, queens, or empress dowagers? Princes and princesses consort?"

Louis XIV: "..."

Other nobles: "..."

Louis XIV swept a glance at the surrounding people, who immediately stepped back and lowered their heads.

Louis XIV said huffily: "People who don't care about etiquette, besides those in high positions, are the country bumpkins. Prince, don't be angry with them; I will deal with them."

Those nobles stepped back a little further.

Yinzhi said: "Then I will trouble the French Emperor. It seems that foreigners do not hold our Great Qing royal family in high regard. Uncle, your navy is not strong enough."

Changtai lowered his head and said: "Yes."

Those nobles stepped back a little further again.

Louis XIV was very displeased. But his displeasure was not directed at the Great Qing’s Crown Prince and Prince Zhixin, but at the group of nobles around him.

Let’s briefly mention Western etiquette here.

The Western Middle Ages were always a feudal lord system; nobles often challenged the authority of the emperor, and a perfect etiquette system had not been formed. Their previous etiquette was basically related to religious rituals.

Nobles began to pay attention to etiquette starting from the Renaissance.

In the 12th century, a priest wrote a pamphlet regulating the behavior of priests, and then the 13th-century Bavarian court imitated this to create a "Court Etiquette," which was the starting point of noble etiquette during the Renaissance.

But the initial formulation of noble etiquette was mostly related to hygiene habits. For example, the noble etiquette formulated by England and the Holy Roman Empire stated that one was not allowed to spit across the table with a "biu" sound while eating.

Behaviors that needed to be prohibited by law were, of course, things that nobles often did at the time.

Imagine you are cutting a steak face-to-face with a noble across the table, the other person’s throat gets itchy, they gather their strength, and with a "tui" sound, a mouthful of thick phlegm flies across the table and lands next to you.

This was the medieval noble.

So when did those pretentious Western noble etiquettes of later generations begin?

It started precisely with this French "Sun King," Louis XIV.

Louis XIV could be said to be the most powerful emperor in the history of the European continent. Other emperors would still be held hostage by nobles, but at the height of Louis XIV’s power, nobles could only fawn over him to seek power and status.

When monarchical power is centralized, etiquette must keep up. Louis XIV built the largest palace in Europe, Versailles, and also wanted to establish the etiquette that could best support his identity as the Sun King.

Louis XIV established rhetoric and elevated European etiquette to every aspect of speech and conduct for the first time; only then did the "medieval noble etiquette" seen in later generations come into being.

Capitalists inherited this set of etiquette. Subsequent European etiquette was just a fine-tuning of the etiquette established by Louis XIV.

China is a land of etiquette. Before Yinreng went on his mission, he naturally had to understand European etiquette in detail. Then he found that the "European medieval etiquette" he had seen on screens and in novels was something Louis XIV was still gathering people to formulate, and his expression was particularly awkward.

It turned out that "European medieval etiquette" didn't exist in the European Middle Ages at all; the petty-bourgeois pretentious etiquette of his second life was all something that only existed during the Kangxi era.

Yinreng noted this down and used it as one of his trump cards.

Without perfect etiquette, these minor nobles didn't know how to show respect to foreign royalty. After being reprimanded, they instinctively felt afraid, standing in the corner like little birds with their necks tucked and wings folded.

Louis XIV looked at the nobles around him, then at the orderly nobles and guards of the Great Qing mission, and his face looked even worse.

Although there was no look of contempt on the Great Qing Crown Prince’s face, Louis XIV could already imagine the disdain the Crown Prince would have for French etiquette when writing to the Great Qing Emperor.

Fortunately, the attendants behind him had been well-trained and looked relatively neat, not causing him to lose any more face.

The clash of etiquette between the Great Qing and France in front of the estate soon reached the ears of other kings and rulers.

They all sighed one after another, feeling very uncomfortable.

It was like a well-dressed civilized person suddenly mixed into a group of barbarians; while feeling ashamed of themselves, they also felt the urge to kill this only civilized person.

Unfortunately, the Great Qing’s navy was quite strong, and their territory was not adjacent to theirs, so they couldn't kill him.

"Let’s see what that Sun King talks about with the Great Qing Crown Prince before making plans."

If Louis XIV fell out with the Great Qing because of this, they could profit from it.

What they didn't expect was that Louis XIV, who was arrogant and domineering in front of them, was actually very gentle and humble toward the Great Qing Crown Prince.

"I let you see a joke." Louis XIV sighed.

Yinreng smiled and shook his head: "Before Uncle became the Sun King, European nobles were each doing their own thing and didn't pay much attention to the emperor, so it’s normal that a unified etiquette wasn't formed. We in China also unified the territory first, then unified the etiquette. Uncle is already the Sun King now, and the etiquette worthy of the Sun King should be in preparation."

Yinreng waved his hand, and Xu Yuanmeng and Chen Tingjing walked over together, cupped their hands and bowed to Louis XIV, then stood up straight with their backs straight.

Yinreng had told them that the etiquette for foreign emperors was different from that for the Great Qing Emperor. They must have the necessary etiquette, but the pride and backbone that should be displayed were even more necessary. So regardless of whether they were civil or military, after bowing, they were to keep their backs straight for him.

Xu Yuanmeng was a Jinshi from the 12th year of Kangxi, a Manchu Bordered White Banner man, with the Manchu surname Shumulu; last year he just became a Crown Prince Zhongyun and a daily lecture record official.

Xu Yuanmeng was talented, well-read in poetry and books, and particularly good at etiquette. As a Manchu of the Upper Three Banners, he had "bitterly" finished the Jinshi exam, was thrown into university by Kangxi, quickly mastered several foreign languages, and joined the Great Qing’s first mission abroad.

Yinreng had arranged a difficult task for him and Chen Tingjing.

Now Xu Yuanmeng and Chen Tingjing, one old and one young, brought out the results of their task—a French version of "Great Qing Etiquette."

Yinreng personally picked up the thick book and presented it to Louis XIV.

Louis XIV looked at the table of contents on the title page, his eyes shining, almost glowing.

Thus, during the negotiations of these few days, Louis XIV didn't talk about Catholicism, didn't talk about the Great Qing’s South China Sea, but only discussed with Yinreng how to imitate the "Great Qing Etiquette" to formulate "French Etiquette."

The kings and rulers who were waiting for Louis XIV and the Great Qing Crown Prince to have a conflict: ???

129. The Third Update, Half-Update [V]

After the Great Qing delegation entered Louis XIV's estate, they didn't leave.

Louis XIV arranged for Yinreng to stay next to him, talking with him all night, and even wanted to imitate the Chinese custom of sleeping feet-to-feet.

Unfortunately, Yinzhi, who was clutching his sword, demanded: "Sleeping feet-to-feet is fine, but add me to the mix."

Louis XIV laughed until he couldn't stand straight.

Having come to regard Yinreng as a nephew, he looked at Yinreng and Yinzhi as if they were his favorite sons; he only found Yinzhi's "offense" amusing.

Louis XIV said to Yinreng, "The Prince of the First Rank must be a son the Great Qing Emperor is particularly fond of."

Yinreng smiled and nodded, "Great Qing princes only become eligible for titles after they marry and move out of the palace; some princes never receive a title in their entire lives. My eldest brother hasn't even been betrothed yet, and he is already the highest-ranking Prince of the First Rank in the Great Qing."

Louis XIV sighed, "A young talent."

He looked at Yinzhi with even more favor: "I have a daughter..."

Yinreng laughed, "Uncle, my apologies, but our Great Qing imperial family, much like yours, is extremely strict regarding royal bloodlines."

Because Europe placed such high importance on the purity of bloodlines, they loved intermarriage, which led to the extinction of several royal lineages. Therefore, Yinreng's "laugh" did not cause Louis XIV any dissatisfaction.

On the contrary, Yinreng's casual attitude made Louis XIV even more satisfied.

His own children were as timid as mice meeting a cat when they looked at him, yet a newly recognized junior interacted with him more like a biological son, which made Louis XIV sigh with emotion.

Yinzhi, the Prince of the First Rank with the rolling eyes, rolled his eyes internally.

What do you call this? My younger brother was raised personally by the Khan Ama and has been coaxing that childish, immature, and moody Khan Ama since he was a child. Coaxing you is just a piece of cake!

Louis XIV gave up on the idea of a marriage alliance and treated Yinreng as an equal, discussing matters of etiquette with him.

Yinreng had "learned" many Western etiquettes from literature and film, and he brought them all out now.

Since these were the very etiquettes Louis XIV had established, they naturally suited his wishes perfectly. Every point of French etiquette Yinreng proposed touched Louis XIV's heart, and Louis XIV's gaze toward Yinreng became even more fervent.

If this weren't the first heir to the Great Qing Empire, he would have wanted to use wealth, land, and princesses to keep this Great Qing prince here and make him his true son.

Louis XIV cast his gaze toward the Prince of the First Rank, Yinzhi.

Yinzhi widened his eyes: What are you looking at!

Louis XIV withdrew his gaze.

While Yinzhi and the others were rotating shifts to use the restroom, he quietly asked Yinreng, "Is the Great Qing Emperor very troubled by this Prince of the First Rank?"

Yinreng immediately laughed out loud, "It's alright, it's alright. Beloved sons are usually the ones who cause their parents trouble."

Louis XIV laughed as well. He had guessed correctly.

Louis XIV said, "But Yinreng, you don't look like someone who would trouble your parents."

Yinreng smiled, "Actually, I also trouble the Imperial Father. My eldest brother and I are probably like one who acts and one who speaks; the Imperial Father finds both of us troublesome."

Louis XIV laughed with envy once again.

If he had read "Romance of the Three Kingdoms," he might have said something like, "If one is to have a son, he should be like Yinreng."

Although Yinreng certainly wouldn't want to be like Sun Zhongmou.

"If one is to have a son, he should be like Sun Zhongmou"—only to send 100,000 troops to their deaths at Hefei. That's far too unlucky.

Louis XIV sighed with emotion, "If only I could have a day to chat with your Imperial Father."

Yinreng said, "Uncle Sun King, like the Imperial Father, needs to sit in charge of a vast empire and it is basically impossible to leave his own territory. The Imperial Father also feels very regretful."

Louis XIV nodded slightly, feeling extremely comfortable inside.

Yinreng was very skilled at flattery, calling him Uncle Sun King one moment and the greatest French Emperor the next; if there was anything France did poorly, it was that France was unworthy of such a great emperor and needed changes; the French nobility was also unworthy of the noble Sun King and needed to have their etiquette redefined... every word hit the mark in Louis XIV's heart.

Regarding this, Yinreng tapped his modern history book and thought, I understand Louis XIV better than Louis XIV himself!

In just half a month, Yinreng, leading the Great Qing civil officials, actually helped Louis XIV finalize the first draft of "French Etiquette."

Louis XIV looked at the thick volume of "Great Qing Etiquette," then turned to look at his own thin "French Etiquette," and his expression was still somewhat unpleasant.

But he could not establish more etiquette because he believed in Catholicism, and his nobles were also believers. Catholicism had its own etiquette, covering every aspect of life, and he could not "overstep."

After the etiquette was established, there were only two days left before the start of negotiations.

It was only then that Louis XIV and Yinreng began to talk about interests and religion.

Their discussion went very smoothly. Yinreng took out the drafted contract, and Louis XIV took one look at it and signed it immediately.

Because the things they were discussing, the questions they needed to probe, had already been concluded while discussing French etiquette.

The spies sent by other countries were so dizzy from listening to etiquette that they completely failed to realize the interests hidden within them.

From the etiquette, Louis XIV learned that for the sake of imperial centralization, the Great Qing did not allow any religion to participate in politics, nor would it allow a single, exclusive religion to appear domestically.

Likewise, through the etiquette, Yinreng told Louis XIV that East Asia and South Asia, including the South China Sea, had always been the private domain of the ancient Eastern nation, having paid tribute to China since ancient times, and China would never allow others to meddle.

Through the tug-of-war over etiquette, both men learned each other's current bottom lines.

The Great Qing was attached to its land and had no interest in expanding territory overseas; the Great Qing only wanted to lease ports and land to build workshops, markets, and conduct business.

Just as the Great Qing helped France establish "French Etiquette," the Great Qing had no interest in other countries and was happy to help them.

However, the area surrounding the Great Qing had been China's backyard since ancient times, and the Great Qing would continue to strengthen its rule and expel outsiders.

Coincidentally, although France had intentions of seizing colonies around the Great Qing, it had not yet taken blatant action. Therefore, if the Great Qing cleared out the surrounding colonies, it would not have much impact on France.

And the Great Qing's willingness to help France—by providing naval support while France waged land wars—would have a huge impact on France.

Looking at it this way, France hadn't really given up anything and yet had gained a powerful ally; why not?

The Great Qing also promised to reduce tariffs with France and become a strategic trade partner.

This would drive those French merchants who did not support Louis XIV and leaned toward the British and Dutch Protestants crazy.

As for Catholicism and the Pope, the Great Qing was too far away; even if Louis XIV wanted to proselytize, he would have to suppress the domestic Protestants first before plotting elsewhere.

When it comes to religion, internal divisions are often more severe than divisions between different religions.

France didn't have the idiom "befriend the distant while attacking the near," but Louis XIV was a qualified politician and strategist; he understood the importance of such a strategy.

In this negotiation of interests mixed into etiquette, Louis XIV felt the sincerity and generosity of the Great Qing Empire and signed the agreement very readily.

After signing the agreement, Louis XIV couldn't help but sigh, "With the Great Qing's strength, it is fully qualified to compete with France for world hegemony."

Yinreng suppressed a laugh. Why did this sound like Cao Cao saying to Liu Bei, "The only heroes in the world are you and I"?

Yinreng said with a smile, "Our Huaxia China has been attached to its land and valued harmony since ancient times; we don't like to go outside and stir up trouble."

The entire Great Qing delegation nodded, "Ah, yes, yes, yes, His Royal Highness the Crown Prince is absolutely correct."

We don't know anything about the Qin Dynasty expanding its territory;

We don't know anything about the Han Dynasty pointing its swords at the desert;

We don't know anything about the Tang Dynasty's 'Heavenly Khan' title;

We don't know anything about the Yuan Dynasty's iron cavalry;

And we know even less about how our Great Qing is currently preparing to find places abroad to grant as fiefs to the princes.

Changtai and Yinzhi nodded slightly with their hands behind their backs in unison: "Ah, yes, yes, yes, we never like to stir up trouble outside."

Louis XIV actually believed it.

He sighed with emotion, "As expected of an ancient Eastern nation."

Yinreng smiled. That's right, that's me!

Yinreng, wearing the kind smile of a benevolent ancient Eastern nation, arrived at the negotiating table.

The Great Qing remained generous and sincere, not at all as fierce and brutal as they were on the battlefield, creating a huge contrast.

Yinreng smiled and told both friends and foes that war is war, and since everyone has different stances, there's nothing to be done about it. But business exchanges are business exchanges, and cultural exchanges are cultural exchanges; the Great Qing very much wants to be friends with everyone.

Besides, we only fought at sea and didn't affect the mainland, so it doesn't count as a life-and-death feud.

The Dutch, whose mainland was attacked: ?

The "won't affect the mainland" you're talking about just means it won't affect the Great Qing's mainland!

Dutch Stadtholder William III gave a bitter smile. This Great Qing Crown Prince looked very young, but he didn't expect his negotiating skills to be so seasoned.

He had originally thought the Great Qing Crown Prince was just a mascot and that the main people in charge were the old men in the delegation. To make the delegation panic, he had specifically requested a certain number of participants, thinking that even if the Crown Prince was reading from a script, he might make mistakes without anyone to prompt him.

But the moment the Great Qing Crown Prince opened his mouth, he knew he was wrong.

He had greatly underestimated this Crown Prince.

William III sighed deeply; although he was unwilling, he was the first to agree to the peace treaty with the Great Qing.

The reason was simple: although the Great Qing refused to budge an inch, the treaty they offered was the most moderate. Even if the Netherlands hadn't been defeated, they might have agreed to the terms—aside from leasing land near the ports—out of friendship (interests) with the ancient Eastern nation.

The reason the Great Qing gave for leasing the land also ensured that William III wouldn't be scolded by the Dutch nobility and the Dutch people.

Yinreng said that the Great Qing would open up trade with Europe, but the people of the Great Qing were truly unaccustomed to Europe.

Your European customs and etiquette are different from the Great Qing's, your living habits are different from the Great Qing's, and more importantly, your Europe is too dirty.

Yinreng said helplessly, "Our cities had sewage systems hundreds of years ago; why do you throw all your trash onto the streets? The Great Qing cannot manage your city's appearance, so we only ask to lease a piece of land to let the Great Qing people build and maintain their own hygiene."

European nobles: "..."

Louis XIV, who had already started wearing high heels, asked, "Yinreng, are your cities really that clean?"

Yinreng said, "I always thought our outer cities were quite dirty, but..."

In fact, the hygiene conditions in ancient Chinese cities weren't that great, at least not in the eyes of modern people; they were very dirty and disgusting.

For example, the Ming Dynasty's "Wanli Yehuo Bian" records of Bianliang: "After the rain, the streets are full of excrement and mud that splashes onto your waist and abdomen; after a long dry spell, the wind blows and dust rises, making it impossible to recognize faces."

But compared to Western Europe, the hygiene conditions of Great Qing cities were considered good.

Although Great Qing cities had soil and water pollution, they at least had sewage systems;

Although people often defecated on the streets in the Great Qing, they would be given forty lashes if caught;

The Great Qing also had people who cleaned and transported excrement, which was a big profit; those who managed a street were called "excrement tyrants," and they were very powerful local snakes.

When a dynasty was in its prime, its administrative capacity was strong, and the streets were relatively clean.

Therefore, the Beijing of the Kangxi era was considered relatively clean. At least in the places where high-ranking officials lived, one could not smell the odor of excrement or trash.

But Western Europe did not use excrement as an important agricultural fertilizer like China did, nor did they have perfect sewage systems during the Middle Ages. Because there was no etiquette to restrain men and women from using the restroom in public, they didn't feel ashamed. Therefore, the poor areas of the Beijing outer city that Yinreng found unbearable were actually considered clean compared to this.

Speaking of etiquette earlier, one of the court etiquettes was that when a noble defecated in his office, others should not greet him.

Isn't that outrageous?

It's not outrageous at all. When their nobles felt the urge, they would just go in a dark corner of the office, and servants would clean it up afterward.

In the Palace of Versailles, which Louis XIV hadn't finished building yet, nobles could also defecate everywhere when they felt the urge, and no one thought there was anything wrong with it.

But in the Great Qing, when Elundai ran to the gate of the Qianqing Palace to urinate, he was beheaded.

Yinreng had been in Europe for so long and found that only before the King and high nobles went out would servants clean the ground to make it look clean; otherwise, sigh, it was beyond words.

"We must have a place to live independently in order to do business with you," Yinreng waved his hands repeatedly. "Wait until you have improved your urban public hygiene, and then we will live with you."

Yinreng was the first to coin the term "public hygiene."

European kings and stadtholders: "..."

They felt insulted.

How were they insulted?

Because the Great Qing Crown Prince told the truth.

William III's mouth twitched, "Very well."

The Great Qing wasn't trying to carve up territory, just for the sake of their subjects' (crossed out) health (crossed out) etiquette and customs; it was no big deal.

As for the Dutch base in Nanyang, the Great Qing had already taken it, and now they were just notifying him; William III had nothing to say.

Now the Netherlands didn't have the ability to maintain that area, and the Great Qing brought out history books to say that it had been Chinese territory and a Chinese vassal state since ancient times, and also told them that even the Zheng family had been reclaimed by the Great Qing; William III had nothing to say even if he wanted to.

Thus, the Great Qing Crown Prince Yinreng ended the negotiations early, rolled up the negotiation agreement, and listened with a smile as this group of European leaders bickered at the meeting.

It seems that negotiations, whether ancient or modern, are the same; they often end in a fight.

Yinzhi, sitting next to Yinreng, kept shifting his butt on the chair; not only was his face filled with "fight, fight," but his body also really wanted to join this brawl.

Yinreng kicked Yinzhi hard to make him be quiet.

They just needed to sit firmly in their position as spectators and not get involved in this group's division of interests on the European continent.

On the first day, Yinreng achieved his predetermined negotiation goals. For the next few days, Yinreng only took Yinzhi and a few guards to attend the meetings as observers, while he sent the other envoys out.

Yinreng brought out a large amount of supplies and had these officials visit the high-level officials of various countries, not to discuss interests, but only to discuss culture and interests, striving to become friends with them.

Yinreng said, "You have already seen that the urban construction here is far inferior to our Great Qing, so why are they our greatest threat? Witness it with your own eyes. This is not bribery; this is making friends."

The Manchu and Han officials of the Great Qing looked at each other, and under Yinreng's orders, they gritted their teeth and took gifts to pay visits.

They wanted to see what kind of skills this group of people, who were making such a spectacle of themselves, actually had to have already seized most of the world's territory.

In the evening, Yinzhi gnawed on a chicken leg for a late-night snack and asked, "Do you think those officials will be able to figure it out?"

Yinreng said, "If they figure it out, they can learn from the excellent aspects of the West; if they don't, they will feel even more frustrated, believing that the Great Qing is stronger than these countries and should be the world hegemon. Either way is fine."

Yinzhi gave Yinreng a greasy thumbs-up, "Your calculations are flawless."

Yinreng didn't know whether to laugh or cry. What flawless calculations? He was just looking at the problem dialectically.

In short, talking nonsense.

Yinreng's goal was just to let them understand the West. As for what kind of thoughts they would have after understanding, one had to understand first.

Yinreng hoped that this group of people could bring the situation in the West to the people of the Great Qing intuitively, rather than listening to the missionaries' nonsense.

130. The First and Second Update [V]

The more William III negotiated, the more he felt that the Great Qing was truly too kind.

He even accepted the Great Qing's reason for joining the French alliance to beat up the Netherlands—you occupied the Great Qing's Taiwan; do you expect us to just chase you away instead of coming to beat you up? There's no such thing as a free lunch.

Look, after the Great Qing finished beating up the Netherlands, they only asked for some war reparations, which could even be paid in grain, minerals, etc.; a treaty for equal and mutually beneficial trade and tariffs; and a small piece of land near the port for Great Qing merchants to live in. They didn't ask for anything else.

Even for the Dutch colonies, the Great Qing only asked for places that were already within the Great Qing's sphere of influence.

Is there any country kinder than the Great Qing?

When William III welcomed the private visit of the Great Qing Crown Prince Yinreng, he identified even more with the Great Qing and Yinreng.

As expected of a land of poetry and etiquette, a mysterious ancient nation with countless legends. For the first time, William III discovered that someone could be as beautiful as a painting, regardless of their face or voice, just by their demeanor.

And this person wasn't just the Great Qing Crown Prince. All the Great Qing envoys were like this.

Especially the two guards behind the Crown Prince holding the ceremonial equipment; they were even more beautiful than any painting.

William III was at a loss for words.

Because the Great Qing envoys were so beautiful, William III's wife, Mary, couldn't help but join William III in receiving the Great Qing envoys.

Of course, Mary and William III had an excellent relationship, and there was no other meaning; it was purely to feast their eyes.

Yinreng glanced at Mary, who was looking at Nalan Rongruo and Cao Yin with stars in her eyes, and introduced them with a smile: "Rongruo is our Great Qing's number one talent; his poetry is copied all over the world. His father's position is similar to your Prime Minister, and he himself has made military achievements on the frontier. He has always been my Imperial Father's trusted guard."

"Ziqing is also a talent, raised under my Imperial Father's watch since he was a child. His father is the Minister of Finance in the wealthiest part of the Great Qing, and he will inherit this position when he grows up."

"Both of them will be dealing with wealth in the future, so I brought them to seek advice from the Dutch Stadtholder."

The way William III and Mary looked at Nalan Rongruo and Cao Yin changed immediately.

Guards are not all the same; some are the trusted aides of emperors and stadtholders and will become important ministers of the country in the future; others are just there for their beauty.

These two were clearly the former.

Mary raised her fan to cover the regret on her face: "Your ministers are truly good-looking."

Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin: "..."

They had been praised for their appearance countless times, but this time they felt deeply offended.

Yinreng explained with a smile, "Having a proper appearance is one of the requirements for being an official, unless that person's talent is particularly outstanding. As the Imperial Father's personal guards, their appearance must be one in ten thousand. Has the Dutch Stadtholder seen any other envoys from our Great Qing who were not properly featured?"

William III thought about the people in the Great Qing delegation and had to sigh, "They are all good-looking."

Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin: "..."

They felt offended on behalf of the ministers in the delegation.

After lightly resolving the awkwardness for Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin and letting William III and Mary know that they should respect these two young men, Yinreng continued to communicate with William III about business.

He was truly here to visit and learn this time, without any ulterior motives.

People might not be familiar with William III, but Queen Mary—people might... uh, not be very familiar with her either.

Then what about the Glorious Revolution in England?

The Dutch Stadtholder William III led troops to land in England, drove away James II of England, became William III of England (William II in Scotland), and became the new King of England together with his wife, Queen Mary.

Their reign laid the foundation for the final victory of the last hundred-year war between Britain and France. It can be said that this future King of England played a decisive role in Louis XIV going from the Sun King to being reviled by everyone in his later years.

After William III became King of England, he also served as the Stadtholder of the Netherlands. Upon arriving in England, he reformed the British fiscal and military systems, utilizing Dutch investments to revitalize the British economy. It is generally believed that William III becoming King of England was the true starting point for Britain's path toward becoming the empire on which the sun never sets.

William III’s military talent was quite mediocre. He was able to outlast France solely due to his extraordinary talent for economics. Yinreng had been coveting his economic prowess for a long time.

At this time, William III was still a frustrated man. He had been defeated by France twice and had signed many humiliating treaties. Although these treaties did not harm the Dutch mainland thanks to the support of his allies, they dealt a massive blow to his political prestige.

William III once considered resigning from his position as Stadtholder of the Netherlands, allowing someone more suitable to succeed him.

Fortunately, the Qing Dynasty's treaty saved him.

The Dutch merchants did not realize that the Qing treaty would harm their homeland; instead, they cheered, excited that they could now do business with the mysterious ancient Eastern nation. They even regarded the Qing’s "lease" as a symbol of deep cooperation with the Qing.

In the future, trade between the Qing and the West would surely pass primarily through the Dutch leased ports, then be transshipped by the Dutch to all parts of Europe. Wouldn't the Netherlands make a fortune!

Because of the armistice treaty with the Qing, William III was able to catch his breath, and his approval rating rose slightly.

Hearing William III’s gratitude, Yinreng almost failed to maintain his gentle, noble, and reserved smile.

He finally understood why those late Qing officials felt smug even after signing countless unequal treaties.

It turns out that everyone is the "late Qing."

Yinreng shamelessly accepted William III’s gratitude, reiterated that the Qing was a benevolent nation, and then asked William III for advice on commerce, specifically regarding banks and national debt.

Yinreng knew the necessity of developing finance in this era of great navigation and trade, but his mind was filled only with basic (middle and high school level) economic theories, and he had no practical experience—he didn't even know how to put his theories into practice.

He could only use his theories to bluff William III, leading William III to mistakenly believe he was an expert, and thus seriously discuss specific and core issues encountered in economic and commercial operations with him.

Just like acting as a mascot during the brainstorming session with scientists, Yinreng was now like a relationship counselor with no emotional experience; most of the time he just listened, and whenever he understood a point, he would immediately take the initiative, using the theories in his head to spout some very correct platitudes.

Cao Yin and Nalan Xingde no longer paid attention to Lady Mary’s gaze, focusing intently on remembering what William III said.

Literati generally have good memories. Yinreng brought them along specifically to be his "secretaries," to cross-reference with his own memory and organize William III’s words to take back to the Qing.

Yinreng wasn't sure if the stagnant Qing would use this set of advanced theories, but he could use them in the Qing’s overseas enclaves first.

After he ascended the throne...

Ha, if he could ascend the throne, then he would talk about promoting it in the Qing.

Thinking of Kangxi’s longevity, Yinreng felt that even if he wasn't deposed, he might not live until Kangxi passed away; even if he did, he would be quite old and might not have the energy to carry out drastic reforms in the Qing.

But this mature theory must be passed back to the Qing. If he couldn't do it, his descendants could; if his descendants couldn't, it could serve as a reference for the heaven-sent heroes who would eventually overthrow the Qing rule.

Yinreng was indeed a perfect communicator. He could make Louis XIV, who had returned to Paris, view him as a nephew, and could also make William III accept him as a friend across generations.

William III later said in his memoirs that, apart from Yinreng, he had never been so happy chatting with anyone else.

This memoir reached Yinzhi, who was still alive and kicking, wandering around the world. Yinzhi wrote directly to Kangxi, demanding that the memoir be listed as a banned book, only to be scolded in a five-thousand-word reply from Kangxi.

When William III talked about economics, he also touched upon religion—in European society, religious topics are always unavoidable.

Yinreng said very sincerely: "England’s shift from Catholicism to Protestantism was simply a refusal to recognize and a wariness of the Pope, an existence with a higher status than the King. The Qing is the same; we recognize that deities have a higher status than the Emperor, but we do not recognize a secular Pope with a higher status than the Emperor. In China, since the Zhou Dynasty, the Emperor has been the Son of Heaven, the only living saint among all religions."

Yinreng was spouting nonsense, but he did so based on the actual situation in Europe, making it sound very reasonable and convincing.

William III immediately thought of Central European countries: "Theocracy? For a country, that might be a blessing."

Yinreng thought to himself, he didn't know if it was a blessing for the country, but it certainly was for the ruling group.

However, China was not a theocracy; rather, it strictly forbade religion from participating in political affairs.

China’s attitude toward religion is difficult for foreigners to understand, just as it is difficult for Chinese people to understand the foreign fanaticism for religion.

Yinreng could only make things up, spouting off Chinese governing concepts like "Son of Heaven," "shepherding the people on behalf of Heaven," "receiving the mandate from Heaven," and "interaction between Heaven and man" to William III.

William III sighed in admiration repeatedly, expressing that he had gained much insight.

Even Lady Mary stopped looking at Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin, turning instead to join the conversation with Yinreng.

The future Queen Mary was someone who didn't like political chores much, but that didn't mean her political skills were weak.

When William III was away fighting France, Queen Mary was responsible for domestic affairs, and her prestige was extremely high.

After Queen Mary passed away, William III’s approval rating in England dropped rapidly. Although this was partly because William III was not of the British royal bloodline, if Queen Mary had not been recognized during her reign, the ministers and the public would not have missed her so much.

Mary was the daughter of James II, who had not yet inherited the throne. She was a Protestant, while James II was a Catholic; the current state religion of England was Protestantism, and Catholics were cruelly persecuted and discriminated against—even the heir to the throne could not be a Catholic.

The current King, Charles II, was old and sickly, and the war of succession had already begun. James II refused to abandon Catholicism, and Mary was already standing in opposition to him.

It is said that there is no family affection in royal families. As a devout Protestant, Mary was also very cold toward "heretics." But humans are not made of wood or stone; how could she have no feelings? Deep down, Mary was still deeply pained by the father-daughter rift caused by religious beliefs.

After hearing the Eastern philosophy on faith, Mary hoped to discuss with Yinreng a way to make her father abandon Catholicism.

Yinreng smiled and said: "The emergence of Protestantism was originally because the Pope was corrupt; believers wanted to believe in God, but not in the Pope. But now that the Church of England controls the government, it is normal for some to oppose it. We have an old saying in China: 'There is a specialty in every trade.' Perhaps the day your religious figures here only concern themselves with religion, this issue will be completely eradicated."

After saying this, Yinreng shook his head: "Right now, it’s too difficult. I’m sorry, I really can’t think of a way."

Lady Mary closed her eyes in pain and asked: "Will there be such a day?"

Yinreng nodded: "If you can drive away the influence of the Pope, you can also drive away the influence of other archbishops on the country. I think there will be such a day; it’s just a matter of time."

William III gave a wry smile: "You trust Great Britain even more than we do."

Yinreng said: "I don’t just trust Great Britain; I trust all of Europe, or rather, I trust the whole world. What is right will eventually be right."

Yinreng paused and added: "I also trust you. I have chatted with the Catholic Emperor of France before, and now I am chatting with you, who believe in Protestantism. Although your faiths are different, there is one point of persistence that is the same."

William III: "Not wanting a Pope above the King?"

Lady Mary opened her eyes: "Not wanting religion to interfere in politics."

Yinreng nodded: "Eastern history is long and deep. If you cannot find the answer in your own history, perhaps you can take a look at the history of the East."

Yinreng gifted William III and Lady Mary a set of Chinese history books, starting from Pangu creating the world.

Your Western history begins with the "Homeric Epics"; our Eastern history doesn't count even if artifacts are unearthed, unless there are written records.

Sorry, the times have changed.

Yinreng shifted the religious topic to exploring history and, on behalf of the Qing, invited the Netherlands to join the Qing in formulating world history.

We of the Qing are a nation of etiquette, and as an ancient civilization, China has always "used history as a mirror," placing the greatest importance on it. Now that the Qing is stepping into the world, we also want to use our civilization to help other countries and peoples become civilized together.

Therefore, we of the Qing are preparing to establish a "World History and Culture Association," inviting archaeologists from all over the world to study history together.

Yinreng’s young face forced a sad and vicissitudinous expression: "Our Chinese history books record many nations that once possessed brilliant cultures. We were not the only ancient civilization. During this mission, I searched for nations that once had brilliant cultures one by one according to ancient books, only to find that most of them have been submerged in the torrent of history."

Yinreng gave several examples of ancient civilizations, and the legendary stories were so captivating that Lady Mary, who had been pained by thoughts of her father, temporarily forgot her sorrow.

When they heard that the people living on the territories of these countries had no idea what their land once possessed, and that only China’s history books remembered them, the couple both wore expressions of sadness.

Yinreng sighed: "People need tombstones after they die. When a civilization dies, whether it fades away naturally or is conquered, leaving them a tombstone and writing an epitaph for them can be considered a form of pity from those who come later. Even for those who conquered them, if they can leave a tombstone for the conquered, it is firstly to show off their own achievements, and secondly, it can be considered a way to appease the local people."

William III was lost in thought.

Yinreng smiled: "If you don't like it, just consider it my ramblings. China is like an old man with a very good memory. As she moves forward, her former friends and enemies have all disappeared into the dust of history. Looking around, it is inevitably somewhat desolate. This is also the reason why China doesn't interact much with other countries. China does not interfere in the internal affairs of other countries, and cannot interfere."

"I watched him build his mansion, I watched him feast his guests, I watched his mansion collapse."

For the last sentence, Yinreng used Chinese, quoting lines from "The Peach Blossom Fan," even though "The Peach Blossom Fan" had not yet been completed.

However, with just these three sentences and no context, Nalan Xingde and Cao Yin just thought Yinreng was expressing his feelings and didn't think much of it, until they heard "The Peach Blossom Fan" later and were filled with question marks.

"The Peach Blossom Fan" describes the events of the late Ming Dynasty and praises those who were loyal to the former Ming. Why would the Crown Prince know the lyrics from "The Peach Blossom Fan" so early?

It couldn't be that the Crown Prince of the Qing was supporting Kong Shangren in writing plays praising the former Ming, right?

This would likely become an eternal mystery.

William III and Lady Mary didn't understand Chinese, but listening to the rhythm of the language, they felt it was particularly beautiful and particularly sad.

Nalan Xingde had his poetry talent maxed out; he could write poems in whatever language he learned. He already had many books of poetry in various languages in his hands.

When William III and Lady Mary communicated with Yinreng, they spoke English, so Nalan Xingde translated those three sentences into English verse.

Foreign poetry doesn't have as many rules as Chinese poetry; for Nalan Xingde, writing poetry was particularly easy.

After he recited the three lines of poetry, William III and Lady Mary gasped and praised him repeatedly.

Lady Mary said: "Is this a poem from your Qing Dynasty?"

Yinreng said: "What I said wasn't a poem, but Rongruo translated it into one. I’ve already said, Rongruo is the most brilliant poet recognized in the Qing today. He can write poems in whatever language he learns. Speaking of which, Rongruo brought translations of his own poems from the Qing."

In foreign countries, it is difficult to explain the difference between "Ci" (lyrics) and "Shi" (poetry), so he just called them all poetry.

Yinreng wanted to use culture to pave the way and establish an elegant and friendly image for the Qing, so naturally, there would be no shortage of Nalan Xingde’s lyrics.

The reason Yinreng translated Nalan Xingde’s lyrics first, rather than Tang or Song poetry, was because Nalan Xingde was still alive.

Letting foreign elites admire Nalan Xingde’s lyrics first was clearly more beneficial to the Qing. Once they understood Chinese poetry, they would naturally go on to learn other Chinese poetry themselves, without Yinreng needing to promote it deliberately.

During the few months that Yinreng became friends with William III and Lady Mary, he gifted them books on Eastern etiquette, history, and poetry. These precious books were taken to England by William III and Lady Mary and were later donated by the royal family to the British Museum, becoming one of its treasures.

Through these seemingly casual and unforced exchanges, Yinreng successfully gained William III and Lady Mary’s recognition of the Qing’s attitude toward religion and secured their support in the Qing’s opposition to the Roman Curia.

When William III and Lady Mary learned that the Pope actually wanted to interfere in the Qing, and that the Qing was going to completely ban Catholic missionaries from preaching, they both expressed that they would do their utmost to support the Qing.

They also completely moved the Qing, an enemy nation, into the position of a friend.

Compared to Catholic France, shouldn't England and the Netherlands, who also loathed the Roman Curia, be the Qing’s natural allies?

But what they didn't know was that while Yinreng was becoming their close friend, the Qing’s First Prince, the Prince of Zhi, Yinzhi, had also become a friend across generations with James II.

"Come, drink!" Yinzhi raised a large glass of red wine.

"Come, cheers!" James II also raised his glass.

The old man and the young man clinked glasses, then downed them in one go. The heroic spirit of it made E'lundai and Gali, who were serving as Yinzhi’s guards, twitch at the corners of their eyes.

Even scoundrels like E'lundai and Gali were worried about Yinzhi’s health.

In the eyes of later foreigners, James II was just a loser who was driven off the throne by the Glorious Revolution.

He was unlucky, cowardly, abandoned by his country, and exiled overseas; he seemed like a useless clown.

But the James II that Yinzhi saw was a firm and brave old soldier.

In fact, James II was exactly that.

When James II was young, the Republicans and Royalists in his country were fighting fiercely; he was imprisoned, disguised himself as a woman to escape to the Netherlands, and later went to France.

At that time, he was not depressed, but like an ordinary person, he joined the French army, and later joined the Spanish army.

When he served in the French army, he became famous for his bravery and military talent, and even the French Turenne admired him greatly.

After returning to England, he served as the naval commander of the Second Anglo-Dutch War and achieved great results; New York was captured and renamed under his command.

The turning point in James II’s life was in the middle of the Third Anglo-Dutch War.

At that time, the persecution of Catholics by the Church of England became increasingly severe; they demanded that any Englishman accepting a military officer position must undergo a ritual of cursing Catholicism. James II angrily resigned from his position as the supreme commander of the navy.

His actions angered Parliament, and Parliament intended to pass a bill to revoke his right of succession to the throne. Charles II, who had no biological children, dissolved Parliament for the sake of James II.

The conflict between James II and the Church of England intensified.

James II: "They want to control the British throne! The Archbishop of the Church of England is a son of a b*tch!"
