154. Two Updates in One [V]

Now that Kangxi had arrived, Yinreng relaxed entirely, lying in bed every day like a salted fish that had lost all its dreams.

Kangxi felt utterly helpless. “You are already this old, why are you still clinging to your Ama’s lap?”

Yinreng swayed side to side wrapped in his little blanket. “Ama, what are you saying? Your son is still young.”

Kangxi sighed, thoroughly resigned to this precious son who had become exceptionally clingy after falling ill.

The Crown Prince was brilliant, and he could harden his heart when necessary, but he wilted completely once the deed was done.

Those eight words could not help but surface in Kangxi’s mind once more:

*Too much wisdom brings harm; too much passion does not endure.*

Recalling how agonizingly the Crown Prince had suffered, Kangxi did not dare to burden him with mental strain any longer. The remaining tasks consisted only of remeasuring the acreage and redistributing the fields, which Kangxi could handle on his own.

This time, the Crown Prince had wielded a bloody blade while the Emperor arrived unannounced traveling light, catching the prominent clans of Zhejiang completely unprepared.

Consequently, when auditing the lands and population, Kangxi obtained figures that were positively shocking.

Before coming south, Kangxi’s understanding of the region had relied entirely on reports from his ministers.

Since the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, registered household counts had remained stagnant, and the amount of reclaimed arable land had expanded very slowly; Kangxi had always assumed this was because the southern population had yet to recover and there was a lack of manpower to cultivate wasteland.

Yet when he arrived on the ground, taking just the outskirts of Hangzhou as an example, lush crops stretched as far as the eye could see—a magnificent, thriving vista.

The land was there, and the people were there, all monopolized by local despots. Kangxi had been thoroughly deceived.

Looking at the ledgers, Kangxi was so furious he laughed: “The Eight Banners enclosed land, causing immense suffering for the people, and yet all that enclosed land ended up in the hands of these people? And this happened even before I took personal charge of the court?”

Cha Muyang did not dare to speak.

Even though he had just taken over as the Hangzhou General, the Emperor would not care when he started his term. He was not a member of the imperial clan; if the Emperor decided to vent his anger on him, he would be finished.

"Back then, Ke Kui and his lot colluded to practice usury. The Bannermen mortgaged their land to them in exchange for capital to lend out. When the commoners couldn't repay the loans, they clashed with the Bannermen. They acquired the land at low prices and still pocketed the kickbacks from the usury—truly a risk-free, guaranteed profit."

Kangxi laughed heartily. If one didn't hear what he was talking about and only looked at his expression, one would truly think he was happy.

"The Bannermen, arrogant and despotic, clashed with the miserable commoners, further highlighting the cruelty and injustice of our Great Qing. Later, the commoners sold their land, their children, and their wives, while the Bannermen, unable to collect their capital or redeem their land because the local officials wouldn't allow them to drive the commoners to their deaths, suffered as well."

"Guaranteed profit, guaranteed profit—from the petty clerks to the prefects, they were all their people. It was a guaranteed profit!"

Kangxi laughed loudly and slammed the account book in his hand onto the table.

"Ridiculous, simply ridiculous! The Bannermen took all the blame, yet they couldn't even afford a meal! Cha Muyang, tell me, are the Bannermen stupid?!"

Cha Muyang’s strong, lean body shrank into a ball, looking extremely pitiful.

How was he supposed to answer? Oh, yes, yes, Your Majesty, the previous Hangzhou General was a complete idiot?

But he himself hadn't discovered the trickery in the account books either!

Cha Muyang thought for a moment and answered honestly: "Your Majesty, perhaps the humble general—your subject—is truly stupid. Even after hearing what Your Majesty said, I still don't understand. Although I banned usury as soon as I took office and made the Banner soldiers honestly farm to support their families, I still know that usury is a way to harm others to enrich oneself. How could the Bannermen get poorer the more they lent? To the point of losing their land?"

Kangxi closed his eyes and leaned back in his chair, breathing heavily.

He now understood why the kings of Europe all had to be well-versed in "economics." If it weren't for the fact that the books he had been studying recently contained similar examples, he would never have discovered the tricks these people were playing.

The Bannermen used land to exchange for silver—wasn't that forced buying and selling? Those forced to buy the land were also victims.

The Bannermen practiced usury—wasn't that the Bannermen's own greed? Those merchants who helped the Bannermen practice usury were also coerced.

The Bannermen couldn't collect their debts and went bankrupt—wasn't that their own fault? The commoners were also suffering...

The contradictions and conflicts were all between the Bannermen and the common people. Those gentry and powerful clans remained hidden, like the house in a gambling den—seemingly not involved, but in reality, they were the ones making a guaranteed profit.

No one knew that those who were truly in the lending business were the gentry and powerful clans. They lent out the silver, took the land as collateral, and then instigated the Bannermen to "invest," eating from both ends.

Good, very good indeed. We, the Manchu barbarians who just entered the pass, how could we ever play against them?!

Kangxi remembered a joking remark the Crown Prince made when he insisted on abolishing the Eight Banners: "The Eight Banners are all a bunch of naive fools. Gathered together, they are just a group of silly, rich, naive fools who will sooner or later be swindled until they don't even have their underwear left. And because these naive fools stay together without any clever people around to imitate, they will only become more and more naive."

After Kangxi asked what "naive fools" meant, he ruffled the Crown Prince's hair into a messy bird's nest and laughed, scolding, "You're the naive fool; the Bannermen are quite clever."

Now Kangxi understood. The Jurchen savages from beyond the pass were great at fighting, but when it came to playing politics and manipulating economics, they were truly no match for these powerful aristocratic families with deep historical roots.

They had been playing mind games for thousands of years!

Yes, the reckless Bannermen were just a group of naive fools who were silly, rich, and especially greedy. They were easy to swindle, yet they thought they were the ones bullying others.

The Eight Banners should be abolished. Break up this group of fools, redistribute them, and re-educate them.

Look at the Bannermen in the capital; they weren't bad, they were becoming more and more shrewd.

Reading makes one wise; this group just lacked education.

Before abolishing the Eight Banners, provide education to the Bannermen so they wouldn't be illiterate, unable to even pick up money if it fell on the ground, and starve themselves to death.

Kangxi opened his eyes and said: "I want to establish schools in the Banner camps."

Cha Muyang was stunned for a moment, not knowing why the Emperor had suddenly jumped from talking about account books to building schools.

But since the Emperor had spoken, Cha Muyang immediately said: "I obey the decree. I also had this intention, to have people teach them to read."

Kangxi shook his head: "Not just reading. Memorizing the Four Books and Five Classics is enough. What they need to learn is the same as what is taught at Peking University."

Cha Muyang knew about that Peking University; he had visited it when he returned to the capital and had even given lectures to the students: "They don't even know a single character; I'm afraid they won't be able to learn like the children of the nobility in the capital."

Kangxi said: "Teach them the simple things. As long as they know how to read and count, they can learn. The Crown Prince is currently gathering people to compile primary and middle school textbooks."

If there was a university, there naturally had to be middle and primary schools.

The Imperial Father who returned to the Eternal Heaven was right: to dilute the status of the Confucian scholars, one must, like in the Spring and Autumn, Warring States, Qin, and Han periods, spark another "Hundred Schools of Thought" contention. Use whoever is capable and make them fight each other.

When they were single-mindedly striving to maintain their academic status, they wouldn't have the heart to stir up trouble and play games with the Qing court.

Simply introducing Western learning was not enough. The word "Western" destined the imports to be undervalued. He should revive the traditional Hundred Schools, absorb the essence of Western learning for his own use, and recreate a new Hundred Schools.

Kangxi rubbed his temples, realizing there was so much to do.

If his son were still lively and healthy, he could have shared half the work with him and wouldn't have such a headache.

Unfortunately, his son's illness hadn't recovered, and he spent every day curled up in bed under a small quilt, acting like a mushroom.

Kangxi missed the First Prince at this moment.

Although the First Prince was infuriating, if he were here, he might be able to make the Crown Prince more lively.

At the very least, if the First Prince were here, when Gu Yanwu wrote a letter rebuking the Crown Prince, he would have stormed Gu Yanwu's door.

But he himself had to worry about many things; even if he had the heart to refute, he couldn't put aside his status and dignity to argue with a great Confucian scholar who held no official position.

Kangxi found that after he asked three questions and got no answers, he lost patience with these officials.

He simply arranged the work, letting the officials follow the script and do exactly what he had laid out.

This was very tiring. Kangxi had to arrange everything properly, otherwise, this group of foolish officials would definitely make mistakes.

Only after seeing those officials did Kangxi realize how poor their abilities were.

Yes, someone who could be a magistrate was at least a Juren, so they were certainly all well-read in poetry and books.

But being well-read did not mean one knew how to be an official. They knew nothing about their jurisdictions, couldn't even understand account books, and some were even innumerate—previously, arithmetic was a necessary skill for Confucian scholars, but now they only needed to know the Eight-Legged Essay.

All the miscellaneous affairs in the prefectural offices were basically handled by hired private secretaries, old clerks, and runners, and these people were all locals, meaning they had intricate ties with the local powerful clans.

After Kangxi understood this, a cold sweat broke out behind his back.

Did these magistrates and prefects, who only knew how to read the books of sages, look exactly like the "sagely emperors who rule by doing nothing"?

Perhaps officials, after passing the imperial examinations, must also undergo re-education before they can serve. Otherwise, if they only knew the Four Books and Five Classics, how could they govern a place well?

This group of Jinshi and Juren only cultivated their character, not practical affairs, and even detested practical affairs. But the practical work of a local official was all mundane—it was built up from every single copper coin and every handful of grain.

Kangxi thought of those local officials who were blocked by the commoners who didn't want them to leave.

Zhao Shilin could manage water conservancy; Shi Shilun was skilled at judging cases; Zhang Penghe prohibited illegal levies... what they did was only a very small part of a local official's practical duties. According to reason, water conservancy, judging cases, and prohibiting levies were all the duties of a local official. But they only did a small part, and it made the commoners reluctant to let them go.

What did this explain? That the commoners knew how to be grateful?

It explained that there were simply too few good officials who understood practical affairs!

He once wondered why some corrupt officials were sent off by commoners when they left office, while some upright officials with good reputations were met with indifference by the commoners when they left?

What did this explain? That human nature is inherently evil?

It explained that an official with a very high sense of morality does not necessarily bring welfare to the commoners!

Look at the "superiors" of these Confucian merchants; which clan didn't have a "clean official" with a high sense of morality and an extremely frugal life?

Those clean officials ate chaff and vegetables their whole lives, perhaps even sleeping on beds made of stacked wooden crates, and didn't have enough money for their own burials after death, needing help from relatives and friends.

Yet their clans were swaggering in the locality, and the Confucian merchants were all wealthier than the state.

This strong sense of dissonance made Kangxi feel very irritable.

When he returned to his temporary residence, Yinreng was curled up in a small quilt, lying under the sunset, flipping through history books.

He was reading Sima Guang's "Zizhi Tongjian."

Kangxi pushed aside his son, who had grown a bit chubby from recuperating and looked soft and childish again, and said: "Don't you dislike Sima Guang?"

Yinreng said: "I do dislike him. Sima Guang is a typical example of a Song Dynasty scholar who cultivated a reputation. He spent his whole life cultivating his reputation, and his mind was only filled with that. The country and the commoners were just tools for him to cultivate his reputation, and even his history book was filled with countless private agendas."

Kangxi said: "Then why are you still reading it?"

Yinreng said: "I shouldn't stop reading just because I dislike him. By reading his books, I can understand the man and understand how the Song Confucians, who were like him in cultivating reputations, gradually became corrupt."

"In the past, not to mention the Confucian scholars of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, nor the Han scholars who sought revenge for ten or a hundred generations, just look at the Tang scholars—who among them couldn't destroy a country by themselves? The Six Arts of a Gentleman covered everything. Even Confucius said, 'Among three people walking, there must be my teacher,' and Xunzi said, 'Blue comes from indigo but is better than indigo.'"

Yinreng shook his head.

"By the time of the Song scholars, they advocated for restoring the past, and even surpassing one's teacher became considered disrespectful. If Confucius knew that this group of people hoped that his disciples would be inferior to him, and his disciples' disciples inferior to his disciples, generation after generation..."

Kangxi chimed in, sighing: "Isn't this the misfortune of the Confucian school?"

Who would want their descendants to be worse than themselves?

If you were to find a random commoner now and wish for them to be worse than the previous generation, you would definitely get beaten up.

Yet this absurd thing was the mainstream ideology of Confucianism now.

You cannot be better than your teacher, you cannot be better than the sages, otherwise, you are not respecting the teacher and the Way.

One might ask, when the sage passed away, he was still lamenting that life is finite while learning is infinite, hoping that his disciples would perfect and carry forward his learning.

Could he have imagined that those unworthy descendants would let his learning end with his own lifespan?

Yinreng nodded: "It is the misfortune of the Confucian school. So, Imperial Father, should we write a letter to the true descendants of Confucius?"

Kangxi said: "The Southern Confucians?"

He frowned and sneered: "Are the Southern Confucians necessarily better than the Northern Confucians?"

Yinreng said: "Of course not."

Later generations always talk about how the Southern Confucians are this and the Northern Confucians are that, as if the Northern Confucians were traitors and the Southern Confucians always upheld the pride of the Confucius clan.

In fact, that was not the case.

In the first year of the Yuanzhen era of the Yuan Dynasty, the Northern and Southern Confucians reunited, ending more than a hundred years of dual-lineage existence. After that, the Duke Yansheng was carefully selected by the Yuan Dynasty from the direct lineage after a thorough study of the genealogy.

The reason why there are still so-called Southern and Northern Confucians is that during the hundred years of division, the Southern Confucians had already developed significant clan power locally and accumulated a lot of wealth. With so many people, it was impossible to abandon their land and property to return to the north.

This was equivalent to other clans and families dispersing to start businesses in various places.

The matter of the Southern and Northern Confucians is clear just by looking at the genealogies of the successive Dukes Yansheng.

This, of course, does not mean there were no good people in the Kong family.

There were those in the Kong family who sacrificed their lives for righteousness. It’s just that those with a high sense of morality certainly couldn't remain Duke Yansheng for long.

The Duke Yansheng was appointed by the Emperor and was the result of internal family fighting.

Yinreng looked at the historical materials left by the Yuan Dynasty, where the Kong family fought like dogs over the position of Duke Yansheng—one day saying this person wasn't of the direct line, the next saying that person's mother had remarried, and the day after saying that person had problems. The Yuan Dynasty verified the direct descendants of Confucius several times.

It was truly a magnificent drama. Yinreng found it very amusing.

"Since you know, why are you looking for them?" Kangxi didn't have much affection for the Kong family.

He would kill those with iron-willed integrity, but he also looked down on those with no backbone.

The Duke Yansheng of the Kong family was appointed by the Song people.

The Song people had soft bones, were servile to outsiders, and persecuted military generals internally. Great Confucians like Ouyang Xiu had bullied Di Qing, the only famous general who could protect the country at the time, and tortured him until he committed suicide.

They lacked the ability to inherit the "strong Confucianism" of the Han and Tang dynasties, and had no merits to establish new theories for themselves. Unable to defeat other regimes, they could only seek the legitimacy of their regime from the "distinction between China and the barbarians."

Confucius being titled "King Wenxuan" and his descendants being titled "Duke Yansheng" were products of this background.

Although Confucius was respected before, the Kong family was only "offering sacrifices," not "extending the sage."

Before the Song Dynasty, China was actually very relaxed about the distinction between China and the barbarians. After all, since the Qin conquered the six states, there was no conclusion on what was Chinese and what was barbarian.

As long as one worshipped the ancestors of Yan and Huang and continued the civilization of Yan and Huang, they were Chinese, not barbarians. Many wise emperors throughout the dynasties had barbarian bloodlines. And many Han people today were once barbarians themselves.

This is the great integration of ethnic groups.

To put it bluntly, why do Han people call themselves Han? Because the Han Dynasty was the first unified dynasty after Qin. This was not a concept of an ethnic group aggregated by blood or geography, but a concept of civilization.

The "Duke Yansheng" appointed in this weak background already carried a hint of absurdity and decay.

Yinreng leaned on Kangxi and said: "There are Kong family members who want to live comfortably by sucking blood on the reputation of their ancestors, but there are also those who want to reform the Kong family and restore the name of the true Confucius."

"They don't want the so-called hereditary titles; they want to use their own abilities to restore the name of Confucius' descendants."

"They believe that the Duke Yansheng cannot represent the Kong family, let alone Confucius."

"Confucius is Confucius; the Sage Confucius can only be represented by himself. All acts of descendants using the Sage for profit are smearing the Sage."

Kangxi raised an eyebrow: "There are such people?"

Yinreng smiled: "Youth is truly wonderful."

Kangxi was helpless: "At your age, can you call others young? What do you want them to do?"

Yinreng said: "Restore the Six Arts of a Gentleman. Our Qing Dynasty's Confucianism, not to mention being better than the scholars of a thousand years ago, at least shouldn't be weaker than them, right? Back then, Confucius could handle a bronze chariot with eight horses by himself."

Kangxi was thoughtful: "Restoring the past?"

Yinreng smiled: "Restoring the past."

Kangxi rubbed Yinreng's hair hard: "Let those young people from the Kong family lead the restoration and integrate Western learning into the original Six Arts of a Gentleman?"

Yinreng said: "Why call it integration? Haven't our ancestors studied those Western learnings? I can see many prototypes of Western learning in history books. That knowledge was ours to begin with."

Kangxi: "..."

Kangxi asked: "Are you sure?"

Yinreng patted his chest: "If you don't believe me, Father, send someone to organize the classics and list everything in our history books related to Western learning. We were the first to discover this knowledge!"

Kangxi: "..." Why did he feel his son was a bit shameless?

But he really appreciated his son's shamelessness.

Kangxi originally thought Yinreng would be decadent for a long time after his heartbreak, but he didn't expect that although his son was lazy, his brain was still thinking about how to completely solve the Qing court's powerlessness against the Confucian scholars.

Kangxi wanted to introduce Western learning and promote the Hundred Schools, while Yinreng directly united with the dissatisfied Kong family members to dig up the roots of the Song Confucians.

With both approaches, the effect would surely be excellent.

"Recovered?" After finishing the serious business, Kangxi rubbed Yinreng's head again.

Yinreng smiled: "Father, do you know what crocodile tears are?"

Kangxi asked: "What is that?"

Yinreng said: "When a crocodile eats other animals, it sheds tears, looking as if it is compassionate. But in fact, it is just because it has eaten other creatures, its body's salt content has risen, and it is expelling the excess salt through tears, while incidentally lubricating its eyes."

"Crocodile tears are synonymous with hypocrisy." Yinreng pointed to his own eyes and said, "Look at this; these are crocodile tears. I will cry, but when it's time to hunt, I won't be soft-hearted."

Kangxi rubbed Yinreng's head again.

He wanted to tell his son, no, these are not hypocritical tears, you are not a crocodile.

But in the end, he just smiled and said: "Very good. To be a Crown Prince, one should have such courage."

Yinreng smiled and nodded, as if the gloom in his heart had been swept away.

He threw away his small quilt and began to help Kangxi handle government affairs. Kangxi's efficiency immediately improved, and he would likely be able to return to the capital next month.

They took the opportunity to write to some Kong family members, asking them to come to the capital to discuss and create a new era of Confucianism.

Of course, Kangxi also issued a decree to recruit talent, summoning the descendants of the remaining Hundred Schools.

Even if the lineages of the Hundred Schools seemed broken, in reality, there were many who studied their teachings and identified with them. They were just hidden among the people, hidden in the shadow of Confucianism, living as if they were Confucian scholars.

The sword Kangxi raised in the south had made some Confucian scholars in the court very dissatisfied.

But when Kangxi issued the recruitment decree, they panicked.

Could it be that the Emperor was disappointed in Confucianism because of those scoundrels in Hangzhou who used the signboard of Confucian merchants?

No, no, no, no, Your Majesty, those are not true Confucian scholars! We Confucian students are not vulgar people who are obsessed with money and business! Your Majesty, please don't be disappointed in Confucianism because of them and doubt Confucianism's loyalty to the Great Qing!

The Duke Yansheng was frantic and hurriedly submitted a memorial, saying he wanted to come to Beijing to talk to the Emperor.

Once the Confucian scholars got anxious, the rolling heads in Hangzhou, Zhejiang, and the long lines of exiles heading to the frontier were no longer an issue.

Anyway, the blade hadn't fallen on them, so why should they empathize with a group of merchants?

They only wrote articles to attack, scolding the merchants for daring to call themselves Confucian merchants after reading a few books; merchants could never be crowned with the word "Confucian."

The Confucian merchants had wanted the clans in the court to stand up for them, but they suddenly realized they had been abandoned.

100,000

155. Two chapters combined [V]

As spring was coming to an end, Yinreng and Kangxi returned to Beijing.

As soon as they returned to the capital, they went straight to the Changchun Garden to stay.

The Empress Dowager and the Empress Dowager had gone to the Changchun Garden early. Seeing Yinreng return, they exclaimed and fussed that Yinreng had lost weight, feeling heartbroken.

Yinreng rubbed against the Empress Dowager and the Empress Dowager, acting like a spoiled child, saying he had indeed lost weight.

Kangxi was speechless.

The Empress Dowager and the Empress Dowager were old, and it was normal for their eyesight to be poor, but Baocheng, do you still want your face?

Pinch the soft flesh on your cheeks and ask yourself, where have you lost weight?

Kangxi tried to tell the Empress Dowager and the Empress Dowager, whose eyesight was poor, that Yinreng had not only not lost weight but had gained several pounds.

Afterwards, he was scolded by the Empress Dowager and chased out the door.

Kangxi stood in front of the pavilion where the Empress Dowager and the Empress Dowager lived, listening to the laughter coming from inside, his hands behind his back, his expression somewhat desolate.

Baocheng was back, so his status in the hearts of the Empress Dowager and the Empress Dowager had dropped.

"Your Majesty, it's raining."

"Hmm."

My heart is raining too.

After Yinreng returned to the capital, his younger brothers were also allowed to be brought to the Changchun Garden.

It was only then that he learned that his third brother had done something big and was almost notorious among the civil officials—Yinzhi refuted the Confucian theory of "interaction between heaven and humanity" and, leading the members of the newly established Academy of Sciences, had built an astronomical telescope.

Now many people thought the sky was round and the earth was square, believing there were immortals in the celestial bodies. And the "interaction between heaven and humanity" was also built on the premise that the stars in the sky were controlled by gods; otherwise, how could they "interact"?

When they saw the moon with their own eyes, many people collapsed and fell ill, and it was said that some even died.

If the moon and stars were just lumps of dirt, then the "interaction between heaven and humanity" naturally made no sense.

Especially the Imperial Board of Astronomy. Their star-gazing techniques met the astronomical telescope, and their breakdown—let's not even talk about it, several went crazy.

Yinreng was speechless: "You... sigh, take it easy. At such a young age, you've already taken on the reputation of driving officials of the Imperial Board of Astronomy to their deaths. What are you going to do?"

Yinzhi leaned against Yinreng and said: "Isn't this just right? Crown Prince brother wielded the butcher's knife against the southern gentry, eldest brother whipped high-ranking officials in the court, fourth brother raided several houses, and I also want to be with my brothers."

Yinreng: "You don't have to be with... what? Little Four raided houses again? Whose houses did he raid?"

Yinzhi was puzzled: "Doesn't Crown Prince brother know? Little Four led people to surround the residence of the Jiangning General."

Yinreng stood up with a "whoosh": "When did this happen?!"

Yinzhi said: "Not long ago? It was when Imperial Father went to Hangzhou, doesn't brother know?"

Yinreng was dumbfounded.

Even he had only killed the gentry and Confucian merchants; he hadn't moved against the high officials in the south yet. How old was his fourth brother? He actually went to surround the residence of the Jiangning General!

That was a General of the First Rank!

Like the Hangzhou General, the Jiangning General was one of the Great Qing's fourteen garrison generals, in command of the Jiangning garrison Banner troops.

The Jiangning Banner compound, also like the one in Hangzhou, was practically an inner city within Jiangning itself.

The Jiangning General's official residence was located right inside the Banner compound. Yinzhen taking men to surround it was the equivalent of charging straight into an army camp to seize the opposing commander.

What kind of fearless death-seeking spirit was this?!

Even his eldest brother, Prince Zhi, wouldn't pull a stunt like that!

Yinreng's knees nearly gave out. "Little Fourth... is Little Fourth alright? No, he must be fine. Ama didn't tell me about this, so he must be safe. I'll go ask Ama!"

Yinreng set off to find Kangxi, dragging his whole retinue of little attachments behind him.

Kangxi looked at the long line of younger brothers trailing behind Yinreng and asked, "What is it? Which little prince got into trouble?"

Yinreng cried out, "Khan Ama! What happened with Little Fourth? Was he hurt?! Who egged him on? How could he be so reckless! Even if he wanted to confiscate a household, he should have submitted a memorial to you first, Khan Ama, so you could find a way to reassign the Jiangning General before doing anything!"

Hearing that Yinreng was talking about this, Kangxi sighed. "I had everyone keep it from you. How did you know... Third Prince?"

Yinzhi poked his head out from behind Yinreng. "Khan Ama, you never told this son I couldn't tell Crown Prince Elder Brother."

Kangxi was struck speechless. He truly had forgotten to instruct this young prince, having only warned the courtiers and palace servants.

"Ah, don't fret, it's already resolved," Kangxi said with a sigh. "As for the Fourth Prince, no one egged him on. He led a band of Banner soldiers to counter-charge the Jiangning General's residence all on his own and tied the general up."

Yinreng was dumbfounded. "How did he manage that?"

"I would very much like to know that myself," Kangxi replied.

When Kangxi had first learned of it, his thoughts had been identical to Yinreng's.

Just how old was the Fourth Prince?!

Yinreng muttered blankly, "Little Fourth's talent for raiding households is truly peerless."

Kangxi's expression turned peculiar. "What kind of talent is raiding households? Does such a talent even exist?"

Yinreng suggested, "A talent for rectifying officialdom? Perhaps the Ministry of Personnel can be given to Fourth Brother later to practice on?"

Kangxi: "...So Little Fourth can tie up all the civil and military officials in the entire court?"

Yinreng was struck dumb.

He smiled bitterly. "Khan Ama, should we recall Little Fourth?"

Kangxi sighed. "The Jiangning General's estate has already been seized, so let him carry on for now." Otherwise, wouldn't the Fourth Prince have taken that risk for nothing?

Kangxi had originally thought the Eldest Prince—who was prone to kicking down the doors of senior ministers—was the most reckless and gave him the biggest headache. Yet now, the Third Prince had hounded an official of the Imperial Astronomical Bureau to death, and the Fourth Prince had incited the Jiangning Banner garrison to storm the general's residence... Truly, each of his sons was more of a "genius" than the last.

Kangxi felt a wave of emotion. Fortunately, the Crown Prince was even more formidable and brilliant than all of them, and had been educated jointly by Khan Ama and himself. Otherwise, who could possibly keep them in check?

Having other princes grow too capable was the root of disaster.

Luckily, oh so luckily, the Crown Prince could suppress them. Kangxi could rest easy and let his other sons display their talents.

Unaware of Kangxi's internal joy and musings, Yinreng held his forehead and asked, "Should I go relieve him?"

Kangxi said, "You rest properly. You've just returned from the south, and after such a severe illness, you..."

Before he could finish speaking, the little princes began to shriek one after another.

"Crown Prince Elder Brother is sick?"

"Wuwuwu, is Crown Prince Elder Brother sick?"

"Crown Prince Elder Brother, go rest quickly."

"Crown Prince Elder Brother, don't be sick." ...

Kangxi sorely wanted to reprimand the little princes to respect their old father and not interrupt him.

But seeing the little princes bawling in a heap, Kangxi's heart softened.

"His illness has already passed, though his body is still somewhat weak. Stop crying. If you cry, the Crown Prince will have to waste his energy coaxing you, making him even more exhausted," Kangxi said sternly.

The little princes clamped their hands over their mouths at once.

Yinreng wiped his younger brothers' tears and snot one by one. "Khan Ama, don't scare them. I'm fine. Ah, alright, alright, I'll rest."

Entangled helplessly by the younger princes, Yinreng had no choice but to write a letter urging Yinzhen to be cautious, abandoning the idea of going to Jiangning to take over the mess.

After receiving Yinreng's letter, Yinzhen stuck out his tongue. "Phew, that was close. I thought Crown Prince Elder Brother would scold me and say he was coming to replace me. Crown Prince Elder Brother still trusts me after all."

Young Yinzhen was thoroughly pleased with himself.

Across from him, Xu Sanli and Shi Shilun, who were flipping through account books, both wore expressions of sheer agony.

It was bad enough that the Emperor indulged the Fourth Prince's wild antics, but how could even the Crown Prince...

Young Yinzhen opened another letter. This one was from the Third Prince, Yinzhi.

Before he had read more than a few lines, he jumped up from his chair. "Crown Prince Elder Brother fell ill?!"

Xu Sanli and Shi Shilun were greatly shocked. "His Highness the Crown Prince fell ill? Is His Highness alright?!"

If anything happened to the Crown Prince, both the imperial harem and the court would be thrown into chaos!

Young Yinzhen finished reading the letter with a tight frown, then said, "Crown Prince Elder Brother fell gravely ill in Hangzhou, but he had already mostly recovered upon returning to the capital. It seems it was from overexertion, combined with grief turning into illness."

"Grief..." Shi Shilun murmured. "What on earth did His Highness encounter that would cause him to fall ill from grief?"

Young Yinzhen gave a cold snort. "The southern gentry and wealthy merchants plotted to incite a riot, using the populace as leverage to force the court to reinstate the Queue Order and the Clothing Order. Crown Prince Elder Brother must have been heartbroken. My Crown Prince Elder Brother is so kind-hearted he wouldn't even step on an ant. Now that rivers of blood have flowed in the south, even if they deserved it, Crown Prince Elder Brother couldn't help but feel sorrowful."

Xu Sanli and Shi Shilun frowned at the same time.

They knew about the events in the south, but neither believed those southern families would do something so foolish.

Hadn't the Queue Order and Clothing Order been pushed by the Manchus? Even if Han civil officials begrudgingly shaved their heads, they were certainly opposed to it in their hearts.

Young Yinzhen remarked faintly, "Back then, your Duke of Yansheng was the first to shave his head, leading the Kong clan to kowtow before the Qing army. Later, during the southern campaigns, it was the surrendered Ming officials and generals whose voices were loudest in demanding the Queue Order. It's understandable; some Han people are even keener on shaving their heads than Manchus."

Hearing Yinzhen's sharp words, both Xu Sanli and Shi Shilun felt quite embarrassed.

The Fourth Prince's remark had a wide blast radius, dragging both of their families into the mud.

Seeing their unsightly expressions, young Yinzhen asked in confusion, "Why are you two angry? Didn't you only become officials after the Qing entered the Pass? You were Qing subjects from the start. Only those with a guilty conscience get angry."

Shi Shilun and Xu Sanli were struck speechless in unison.

So if we get angry, it means we're admitting we have something to hide?

Shi Shilun smiled wryly. "The Fourth Prince is correct. It truly has nothing to do with this subject."

My family weren't surrendering generals from when the Qing first crossed the Pass; they only surrendered later.

Xu Sanli said stiffly, "Indeed, it has nothing to do with this subject either."

I obtained my jinshi degree during the Shunzhi reign, making me a Qing jinshi. What does that have to do with the former Ming?

Young Yinzhen nodded repeatedly. "Right, right, right, it had nothing to do with you to begin with. Ah, help me think of how to reply to Crown Prince Elder Brother so he won't worry about me. He's only just recovered from his illness, he mustn't fret over me."

Shi Shilun and Xu Sanli exchanged a look, both roaring internally.

Fourth Prince, if you don't want His Highness the Crown Prince to worry, then don't be so reckless!

A mere child with his hair in twin tufts had led a group of Banner troops to storm the Jiangning General's estate! When they first heard of it, their minds had nearly collapsed; they had no idea how the Fourth Prince had pulled it off right under their noses!

Everyone said Prince Zhi was constantly astonishing, but the Fourth Prince was hardly trailing behind.

The Third Prince hounded an Imperial Astronomical Bureau official to death in the capital?

Just an astronomer; that paled in comparison to the Eldest Prince and Fourth Prince.

Far away on the grasslands, Prince Zhi, Yinzhi, also received Yinreng's reassuring letter and Yinzhi's tattle-tale report.

When Yinzhi learned that Yinreng had been gravely ill, he nearly dashed straight out, wanting to ride his horse back to the capital.

However, Kangxi's handwriting following the Third Prince's letter brought him to a halt.

Kangxi informed Yinzhi that Yinreng had long since recovered and had even put on some weight. He told Yinzhi to focus on his own duties with peace of mind; returning now would only disturb Yinreng while he was recuperating.

In the letter, Kangxi also lamented that the Crown Prince was too soft-hearted, grieving to the point of fainting over the execution of a batch of would-be rebels. Although the Crown Prince hadn't stayed his hand in handling the matter, Kangxi was still worried and hoped Yinzhi would counsel the Crown Prince more often.

Yinzhi gave a cold snort. "You need me to counsel him on everything—what use are you as an Ama!"

The people around Yinzhi kept their eyes on their noses and their noses on their hearts, pretending not to hear Prince Zhi's insolent words.

Yinzhi knew that Yinreng would likely soon discover the Third Prince had tattled, and would write to explain the truth to him.

Sure enough, a few days later, he received a new letter from Yinreng.

In the letter, Yinreng admitted to having fallen ill.

"Elder Brother, in order to nail them to the pillar of shame and make the local populace despise them, thereby severing their regional influence, I fabricated this false accusation and deliberately cut off grain supplies to force them to reveal their true colors. Even though I was mentally prepared, once it was accomplished, my heart was still ill at ease. How hypocritical of me."

Yinzhi frowned. How could he put such things in a letter? His younger brother was still far too incautious. If someone discovered this, who knew how much of a storm the words "false accusation" would stir up?

Even if the letter was delivered by Khan Ama's people, his brother shouldn't have trusted them. What if Khan Ama had a lapse of sanity, wanted to harm him, and used this letter as evidence to ruin his reputation throughout the court?

Yinzhi burned the letter, suppressed his urge to rush back immediately, and picked up a brush to write.

He didn't write to Yinreng; instead, he wrote to Gu Yanwu.

He decided he would write to scold Gu Yanwu every few days.

The southern gentry were guilty of monstrous crimes. My brother acted on heaven's behalf and pleaded for the people, yet you dare scold him? Just wait, I'll curse you to death!

You say my brother slandered them? Heh, on what basis do you say he slandered them—show me your evidence! Just because those people are literati and write good essays, they couldn't possibly be wicked? Ridiculous!

You, Gu Yanwu, are nothing special!

Hypocrite!

Yinzhi didn't care whether Gu Yanwu read his letters or not; his men would simply slip them through the door crack or toss them over the courtyard wall.

Even if Gu Yanwu moved, as long as he was still on Qing territory, Yinzhi would be able to send letters to harass him.

While Yinzhi was writing abusive letters to Gu Yanwu, Gu Yanwu had already received Yinreng's letter.

The heading of the letter read: "Petition to Become a Disciple of Master Gu Yanwu."

Frowning deeply, Gu Yanwu smoothed out the paper.

He was profoundly disappointed in Yinreng.

The southern gentry may well have deserved punishment, but Yinreng should not have used the immoral means of slander and coercion to achieve his goals.

Gu Yanwu did not believe that, with Yinreng's intelligence, he couldn't have found real evidence to purge the southern magnates through proper, upright channels.

A Son of Heaven should walk the Kingly Way, remaining upright, candid, and magnanimous, as radiant as the sun.

Schemes and underhanded plots only warped a person's nature.

If the Crown Prince achieved his ends through slander and coercion this time and tasted the sweetness of success, would he continue doing so in the future? Seeing this, would others imitate him? If so, wouldn't the Qing officialdom become riddled with sinister conspiracies?

For petty men, it was better to kill by mistake than let a culprit slip away;

But for a Son of Heaven, it was better to let one slip away than to tarnish his glorious image.

Thus, Gu Yanwu had severely rebuked Yinreng, fearing the youth's moral character would be corrupted.

He even suspected whether these deeds had been carried out behind Yinreng's back by those around him.

Was it that bondservant Cao Yin, or those flattering Han generals? Or perhaps those two young Manchus?

Though he hadn't met Yinreng often, he knew the prince was fundamentally kind and shouldn't have had the stomach for such deeds.

Gu Yanwu had waited for the Crown Prince's letter, yet now he didn't know whether to feel disappointed or to sigh.

In the letter, Yinreng admitted that this interlocking web of schemes had all originated from his own hand; even now that the dust had settled, the executors still didn't know his true objective.

"I must sever the southern gentry's ideological control over the southern commoners. I must leave them thoroughly discredited and strip them of all dignity."

"I know this is drinking poison to quench thirst, but the only one poisoned to death is myself."

What Yinreng hadn't written explicitly was that the one poisoned to death might not just be him, but potentially the Great Qing dynasty as well.

But what did that matter?

He had to awaken those common people, snapping them out of their blind trust in the gentry and powerful clans.

Only then would they learn new things.

Kangxi only thought of the Bannermen. But Yinreng intended to push the "New Hundred Schools" across the entire Qing, especially the culturally prosperous south.

The south placed far more emphasis on Neo-Confucianism than the north, and the local gentry loved opening private academies, monopolizing basic local education.

Furthermore, at the start of every dynasty, an "equal-field system" would be instituted to divide land evenly among the commoners. Only in the twilight of a dynasty, when land annexation ran rampant, would the people be driven to misery, leaving the dynasty unable to collect land taxes.

Yet after the Qing entered the Pass, they had been deceived and failed to carry out a grand reshuffling of land ownership, never dividing land among the commoners. Land annexation was already severe by the Kangxi reign.

Originally, Kangxi had assumed land annexation was due to Manchu land enclosures. Only now did he realize that, despite having enclosed land just over twenty years ago, most Manchus were currently impoverished, barely scraping by on the meager rations provided by the imperial court.

Lacking education, they couldn't even hold onto the wealth in their hands.

By eliminating these powerful clans and distributing the land to the commoners, the people would have a way to survive, and at least during the Kangxi reign, the Qing would be able to collect land taxes in Zhejiang.

If judged strictly by their original crimes, these people did not deserve death.

It was ironic: had Yinreng not used the grain cutoff to bait the gentry into a price war with the "Hua family" and incited public fury, even if they had stirred up unrest, the Qing would still have shown them leniency, executing only one or two. Their clans would not have fallen, and the land would never have reached the Qing court's hands.

Now, the court was forced to execute them, because the commoners had besieged their estates and clashed with their thuggish servants.

Yinreng had incited a genuine riot, and he too had used the populace as leverage.

The more Gu Yanwu read, the more distressed he became.

He didn't understand why Yinreng was in such a rush.

Even if he couldn't kill those parasites now, Yinreng was still young; as long as he kept his eyes on them, he would eventually bring them down through righteous means.

Even if he couldn't bring them down, so long as they were kept in check, they posed no threat to the Qing's rule.

Striking the mountain to shake the tiger was enough—why burn down the entire mountain?

Compared to distributing some land to the people and dispelling the local magnates' influence, the gentry were the very foundation of the state.

Securing the realm lay in winning the hearts of the people, and the key to the people's hearts lay in the hearts of the literati.

If the Crown Prince lost the support of the literati, let alone how he would govern in the future, his very position as heir apparent might not remain secure.

Gu Yanwu truly could not fathom why Yinreng was so impatient.

After burning Yinreng's letter, he said dejectedly, "It seems I am destined not to be the Emperor's Teacher."

He could not accept Yinreng's methods.

Those of different paths could not make plans together.

...

Tang Zhen had just returned to Taiwan when he received letters from Kangxi and Yinreng, learning about what had happened in the south.

The expression on his face was rather peculiar.

Yinreng's actions aligned closely with his own philosophy.

He believed that the people's hearts did not lie with the literati, but with the true commoners. Those officials, every one of them devoid of ambition and exploiting the masses, were the root cause of a dynasty's ruin.

After reading books written by some unknown great sage, Tang Zhen had become even more convinced of the correctness of his ideas.

Yes, this was class oppression!

Although he could only let nature take its course for now, someone in the future would surely change this world full of oppression.

In a hundred years, two hundred years, five hundred, or a thousand years, the wrongs of this world would certainly be set right.

For the Crown Prince to strike at the gentry and divide the land among the people was already an extraordinary feat. As for the Crown Prince's inner torment, Tang Zhen felt it was entirely unwarranted.

How had the Crown Prince merely been testing those gentry and merchants? He had clearly been giving them a chance.

If, when grain prices soared in Hangzhou, those gentry had lent a hand like the "Hua family" and sold grain at fair prices to give the commoners a way to live, the Crown Prince would definitely have spared them.

Yet what had they done?

When everyone in Hangzhou thought the imperial court would dispatch a grand army, they had still hoarded goods to corner the market, intent on making that wicked, blood-soaked fortune.

Why hadn't they been afraid?

Wasn't it precisely because they believed that even if the Qing army arrived to put down a rebellion, their interests wouldn't be harmed?

Hadn't they assumed that even if the truth came to light, their foundation would remain untouched?

Landlords were capitalists too; for the sake of profit, they would even dig up their own ancestral graves.

Tang Zhen sneered. "I'm going to the capital. There must be someone by the Crown Prince's side to protect him. That old fossil Gu Yanwu—what is he, a fart!

Gu Yanwu actually dared to write a letter rebuking the Crown Prince, making him so miserable? Just wait, I'll write and curse him to death!

The Crown Prince is kind and respects his teachers, so he won't do anything to you, Gu Yanwu.

The Emperor cares about his face, so he won't intervene either.

But did you think there was no one else to protect the Crown Prince? Incompetent as I, Tang Zhen, may be, I can still wield a pen to write essays.

You have a pen like a blade, and I have a pen like a blade too.

Come on, let's see whose blade is sharper!

And so, having concluded his world travels, Imperial Preceptor Tang Zhen entered the capital with grand fanfare, formally stepping into the court under the titles of "Emperor's Teacher" and "Crown Prince's Teacher," becoming the preeminent Han minister after Du Lide.

The Han ministers in the imperial court, who had been arguing fiercely over Kangxi's "New Hundred Schools," were completely baffled.

Who was this Tang Zhen? On what basis had he climbed over our heads?

No, I refuse to accept this!

Tang Zhen sneered. You don't accept it? Fine, I'll set up a platform at Peking University to take on all challengers, following the example of Zhuge Liang debating the scholars!

This grand debate by Tang Zhen against the assembly of scholars had an exceptionally far-reaching impact on later generations.

History would record that Kangxi's "New Contention of a Hundred Schools of Thought" began with Imperial Preceptor Tang Zhen "debating the assembly of scholars."

After Tang Zhen refuted the host of civil officials and Confucian masters, disciples of the New Hundred Schools took Tang Zhen as their idol and flocked to the capital one after another.

Once these disciples of the New Hundred Schools arrived in the capital, they also set up debate halls at Peking University to propagate their ideas.

Peking University became like the academies of the pre-Qin era, a battleground where a hundred schools contended.

Thereafter, Confucianism never again enjoyed its former exclusive dominance in the imperial court.

However, Confucianism was not entirely without the power to fight back.

Amidst the debates, a group of sword-bearing disciples of a New Confucianism rose to prominence. Calling themselves the "Militant Confucians," they took up the banner of reviving the Confucianism of the Han and Tang dynasties, taking on both the Hundred Schools and the "Frail Confucians," refuting outdated Confucian dogma, and even opposing the Duke of Yansheng's Kong clan.

The emergence of these Militant Confucians terrified the literati even more than the New Hundred Schools did.

...

...

"The Master said, 'To sacrifice to spirits other than one's own ancestors is flattery!'"

...

"'To sacrifice to spirits other than one's own ancestors is flattery!'"

"'To sacrifice to spirits other than one's own ancestors is flattery!'"

"'To sacrifice to spirits other than one's own ancestors is flattery!'"

Standing outside the human wall, Duke of Yansheng Kong Yuqi nearly collapsed upon hearing these words.

His lips trembled and his face was utterly bloodless as he repeated over and over, "Unfilial descendants, unfilial descendants! I will strike them from the Kong genealogical record!"

Kong Yuqi had inherited the title in the sixth year of the Kangxi reign.

He was fond of painting and loved poetry and literature, resembling not a master of Confucian classics, but rather a romantic poet.

He frequently submitted memorials to Kangxi, none of which concerned education or the people's livelihood, but were solely about "expanding forest lands, stationing guards, exempting rents and taxes, and establishing a hundred-household company."

Our Kong family wants more land!

Our Kong family wants to raise our own private guards!

Our Kong family won't pay taxes!

Furthermore, establish a separate official post of 'Company Commander' just for our Kong family, solely to protect us!

To win over the civil officials and the hearts of the literati, Kangxi had pinched his nose and agreed to it all.

Later, he wanted to renovate the Temple of Confucius and demanded that the laborers dredging the Yellow River be sent to his estate for corvée duty.

Kangxi had agreed even to such an absurd demand.

Kong Yuqi's conduct was entirely that of an insatiable, tyrannical local bully.

If the Qing court only revered Confucius and no longer revered the Kong clan, how could the Kong family continue living their lavish days?

Were they going to make him sit for the imperial examinations? The examinations didn't test painting and poetry!

On the stage, the young Kong clansman had already spotted the nearly fainting Duke of Yansheng, his expression full of contempt.

He cupped his hands toward the assembled literati below: "Since the title is 'Yansheng'—extending the Sage—it means the Sage's descendants carry on his thought. Even if they are not sages in every generation, they should at least be moral gentlemen. Rather than arguing here over whether to continue supporting the Kong family, why not have the court investigate whether the Duke of Yansheng's household can shoulder the heavy duty of perpetuating the Sage's reputation?"

He swept his gaze across the scholars below. "If the Kong family is morally bankrupt and utterly unlearned, are you willing to let such people tarnish Sage Confucius's good name? Or have you already decided that Sage Confucius's descendants are bound to harbor filth, and so you indulge this corruption? Do you truly believe that morally degenerate and incompetent scoundrels are the kind of descendants Sage Confucius ought to have?"

Among the literati debating him, some were struck dumb, while others grew hot-headed: "Let the court investigate! The Qufu Kong family are naturally all moral gentlemen!"

When someone shouted this, Kong Yuqi's vision went dark, and he fainted right away.

Other literati hurriedly moved to cover their hot-headed companion's mouth.

Shut your mouth!

The Qufu Kong family and the Duke of Yansheng were moral gentlemen? What kind of joke was that! Would moral gentlemen be the very first to kneel and shave their heads?

Any scholar with half a brain knew what sort of creatures the Dukes of Yansheng were.

Yet they insisted on revering these creatures, because they hoped to become like them themselves.

In truth, there were no longer any true great clans; the great aristocratic families had already disintegrated back in the Tang dynasty.

Now, there were only local magnates, gentry, and temporarily formidable local despots—none of the old glory where "dynasties come and go, but the great clans stand eternal."

Yet all magnates and gentry yearned for those great clans of old, hoping to become one themselves.

The Kong family was currently the only "great clan" surviving to this day that received worship generation after generation. They were everyone's dream, the imperial court's signboard showing its willingness to nurture scholars.

Look, even if the Kong family was morally bankrupt and unlearned, they could still flourish across generations. This was buying the horse bones for a thousand pieces of gold!

Even the magistrate of Qufu was hereditary, held by the Kong family generation after generation; Qufu was practically the Vatican of China.

"Elder Brother, since when was the post of Qufu magistrate made hereditary for the Kong clan?" Yinzhi asked softly, having disguised himself as a scholar alongside Yinreng to watch the commotion from the crowd.

Yinreng replied, "Since Emperor Yizong of Tang."

Yinzhi remarked with admiration, "'Yizong'? That's a super good posthumous title. He must have been very impressive."

Yinreng gently pinched his younger brother's cheek. "Third Brother, if Father heard you say that, he'd be angry enough to make you copy the Old and New Books of Tang a hundred times."

Yinzhi was dumbstruck. "Ah? D-d-did I say something wrong?"

He racked his brains, completely unable to recall who this Emperor Yizong of Tang was.

He was currently reading the Old and New Books of Tang, but he couldn't memorize every single emperor's temple name!

Yinreng sighed. "Emperor Yizong of Tang was a fatuous and tyrannical monarch. Though the dynasty didn't fall during his reign, the Tang's demise was entirely due to him; he is universally recognized as the indirect cause of the dynasty's fall."

Yinzhi was stunned. "Then how could he be called Yizong? Was 'Yi' not a favorable posthumous title in the Tang dynasty?"

Yinreng replied, "No, 'Yi' was a top-tier favorable posthumous title in the Tang. Aside from Emperor Yizong, only one other person in the Tang had 'Yi' as a temple name: Li Tianxi, the ancestor of the founding emperor Li Yuan, who was posthumously honored as Tang Yizu."

The posthumous title Li Yuan chose for his ancestor was naturally of the absolute highest caliber.

Since then, no descendants of the Tang Dynasty used "Yi" as a temple name, and in later generations, it was at most added to that long string of "posthumous titles."

Who would take a temple name meant for an ancestor and use it for themselves? Only the civil officials who drafted the temple names would do so if they believed the virtue was sufficiently high.

For example, Kangxi's "Shengzu" (Holy Ancestor). Although he didn't deserve it in original history, in the minds of Qing officials and Yongzheng, Kangxi's merits and virtues were sufficient among Qing emperors to be called "Sheng," so they used the temple name meant for posthumously honoring an ancestor for him.

So, does Emperor Yizong of Tang, Li Cui, deserve it?

He deserves it, he deserves it immensely. After all, he allowed the descendants of Confucius to inherit the position of Qufu County Magistrate for generations. With such respect for Confucius, why wouldn't he deserve it? The civil officials were just being thin-skinned for not conferring "Shengzu" upon him.

By the Jiajing era of the Ming Dynasty, the magistrate surnamed Kong was unlearned and morally corrupt. Some ministers could no longer bear it and submitted memorials, hoping to bring Qufu under the direct administration of the imperial court. Emperor Jiajing had the intention to cancel the Kong family's hereditary privilege to the Qufu magistracy, but was met with "death-defying remonstrances" from the majority of civil officials.

Let the people of Qufu suffer, right? Isn't it just being saddled with a trashy magistrate for a few hundred years? Is this more serious than the fact that the Kong family's land was being managed by someone not surnamed Kong, causing the descendants of the Sage Confucius to lose face?

It is not serious at all.

The Qufu County Magistrate must be a member of the Kong family!

Even an iron-willed person like Emperor Jiajing had no choice; he only replaced the magistrate with another member of the Kong clan, and the matter was settled just like that. The previous magistrate faced no consequences, and no one dared to hold him accountable.

Therefore, the Kong family had controlled Qufu for hundreds of years and had long been accustomed to treating the people of Qufu as their servants; how could they not have instances of moral corruption?

They did, they had many. But the victims didn't dare to speak out.

Once they spoke out, it would mean offending the Kong family, offending all the scholar-gentry, and offending all the intellectuals in the world.

In an era where only studying for the imperial examinations could change one's fate, this was equivalent to sentencing an entire clan to death.

Offending the Emperor would at most lead to beheading or exile, but offending the Kong family meant never being able to rise again for generations.

Yinreng almost laughed out loud.

In the midst of the argument, everyone lost their heads; the "Weak Confucians" were actually jumping up and down demanding an investigation into the Kong family to prove that the descendants of Confucius were also sages, and to prove that Qufu under the Kong family's rule was like a Great Unity society.

The firewood had already been stacked, and after lighting it, they even poured oil on it.

This scene was already beyond control.

Yinreng slowly retreated to inform Kangxi of the lively scene.

The people in the arena had red eyes and were worked up, having completely lost their reason.

Now, the voices of the "Weak Confucians" demanding an investigation into the Kong family of Qufu were actually louder than those of the "Strong Confucians."

They not only demanded a thorough investigation but also said that if it were found that the Kong family members were moral models, they would make these "Strong Confucians" commit suicide.

The Strong Confucians were not only unafraid but also said they would join the investigation, and if they had slandered the Duke Yansheng, they would hang themselves at the Duke's gate—extremely fierce and unyielding.

The New Hundred Schools, seeing the Strong and Weak Confucians arguing so fiercely, and adhering to the principle of joining in on the fun, also jumped into the fray to make bets.

Come, come! If the Duke Yansheng's family is truly morally flawless, we will immediately disband our own schools, have our leaders hang themselves at the Duke Yansheng's gate, and the rest of us will change our banners and immediately serve the Duke Yansheng as masters, becoming his servants!

……

Kangxi was stunned: "Hang themselves at the Duke Yansheng's gate?"

Yinzhi nodded vigorously: "That's what they said! They are so fierce and unyielding!"

Yinreng suppressed a laugh: "Indeed, fierce and unyielding."

Hanging themselves at the Duke Yansheng's gate, hahahaha, what kind of dark joke is this? It's killing me.

Kangxi's face twisted severely.

He wanted to laugh, but felt it wasn't appropriate, so his face kept twitching: "Very, very good, very fierce and unyielding. I will personally take a trip to Qufu to thoroughly investigate the affairs of the Qufu Kong family and restore their innocence."

Yinreng laughed: "Father Emperor, you must send more great scholars and civil officials, especially those who stand on the side of the Kong family, otherwise be careful that someone says you are persecuting the Kong family."

Kangxi said: "Of course, I will send the most upright and incorruptible people. It's a pity Chen Tingjing is still in Russia."

Yinreng laughed so hard he couldn't straighten his back: "Hahahaha, Father Emperor, don't be like this, don't persecute Master Chen, hahaha."

Kangxi said sternly: "How is this persecution? It's just an investigation."

Yinzhi also nodded vigorously: "That's right, just an investigation, why are you laughing, Crown Prince brother?"

Yinreng was still laughing, while Kangxi looked at his third son's confused expression and couldn't help but sigh and rub his brow.

Why is the Crown Prince laughing?

I want to ask why you aren't laughing!

Isn't this matter funny!

Kangxi suspected that his third son had a problem with his brain, perhaps inexplicably foolish in some aspects.

Kangxi changed the subject: "It is decided then, I will set off for Qufu tomorrow. You stay behind to help me maintain order. After the Qufu matter is investigated, the capital will surely be in chaos for a while."

Yinreng stopped his wild laughter and said seriously: "I obey the decree!"

‎
